Gentlemen (in chorus): "Oh, no; we can't swim at all." Lady: "Then I think I'll go with you, for in that case you. are sure to be careful." "DOCTOR, what is the meaning of the peculiar formation just at back of baby's ear?" 'Com- bativeness, perhaps." "Why, some one said it was love of domestic life." "Tell me, quick, my dear—what is it?" "It is a little noisy," assented the landlady ; "but from the front veranda one has such a fine view of people who miss the trains," she added, with an air of triumph. A wITTY old American judge, who had spent an evening with a young lawyer in the country whose office was in the second storey, on taking his de- parture, stumbled on the stairs and fell to the bottom. The young lawyer, hearing the noise, rushed out, and seeing the judge lying on his back at the bottom of the stairs, hastened down, and with great anxiety asked, "Is your honour hurt ?" "No," said the judge, scrambling to his feet, "but my legs are." IN connection with the announcement of the birth of a child to the Countess of D--, a paper recalls the following incident connected with the birth of its father, the present earl. An old friend of the family called at the town residence in Park Lane to learn the news. "Is it a boy ?" he asked the gorgeous flunkey who opened the door. "No," quoth James. " Wnat, is it a girl?" "No, sir." The old friend became much interested. "Bless me, then, what is it?" The flankey proudly re- sponded—" It is a heir." THERE is a young member of the diplomatic corps in W-- who is disposed to be polite, but who is not always judicious. He was conversing with a lady who combines intellectual and physical graces with a considerable degree of maturity. "1 have enjoyed talking with you very much," he said. "It is a pleasure to be in the society of some one who has observed the world." "Bat, Mr. Brown," she said, laughingly, " perhaps lam not as old as I look." "I was always sure of that,' he returned with all the gallantry of manner he could muster. "Do you keep overcoats here ?" he asked, as he stopped in front of a c calling store. "Of course ; vhalk right in. I haf der best assortment in der town." " I want to ask you a plain question. and I want a square answer." "Certainly." "Have you an overcoat for two pounds? A YoUNG married lady had just acquired a new coact' and a new footman to mktch. "John," she said ice day, "we will drive out to make a few calls. But I shan't get out of the carriage ; you will, therefore, take the cards that are on my dressing table and leave one of them at each house we etep at." " Very good, ma'am," answered John, Kea ian upstairs to fetch the cards. After they bad driven about a considerable time, and cards had betel left at several houses, the lady remarked :—" Now, we must call at Dale's, Frampton's, and Clarke's." "We can't do it I" here broke in the footman in alarm. "I have only the ace of spades and the ten of clubs left I" Timis was a brass band on board the boat, and white the hand was in the middle of a grand piece of music, a small boy securtd a conspicuous position in front, of the players and began sucking a lemon. He acted au as to attract the attention of several of the players, who seemed to be unable to avoid watching the urchin as he pulled away at the soar 1 fruit. Now, everyone knows how the sight of a lemon makes one's inotith water, and that is just what mu-icisns wish to avoid. The harder the boy sacked the lemon the more watery became the mouths of the players, and finally they had to stop to clean their instruments, and the leader of the band had the boy removed. The youngster claimed he could stops brass band every time with ne lemon.

Of Mr. Fiats, it has been said he is essentially the tarmer-poet.--ha who has been most successiuliii capturing the spirit of beauty in the clearing, the furrow, and the harvest-tieid. The lady Doctor of Science,3Miss May Ogilvie, who received last week her degree-from the Loudon University.. has had an exceptionally brilliant career. She is the daughter of Dr. Ogilvie, of Gor- don's College, Aberdeen. Whilst quite a school girl she obtained a scholarship of £lOO and the dux medal of her college. For some time she studied Music under Dr. Mackenzie with remarkable suc- cess, and WOO became his most promising pupil. In 1889 she passed her B.Sc. with flying colours, and wok another Gold .\ledal—this time as head of Pro- fessor Ray Lancaster's class. ,

Uneated with her numerous victories she next cast envious eyes on the degree of Doctor of Scioace. l'o obtain this, some perfectly original work was necessary, and Miss Ogilvie's selection was• Alpine geology. Her first move in this direction was characteristic of her sex. She designed for herself a graceful Alpine costume which, we are assured by those that have been lucky enough to see her at work, puts the Girl in the Karpathian's garb com- pletely in the shade. Bidding farewell to her friends she disappeared for a couple of years into the South Tyrol uoloinites, from whence she re- cently emerged with the " copy " which got her well-earned degree.

Miss Ogilvie, with her frank, pleasant face, and girlish manner, is quite the antithesis of the con- ventional idea of the blue stocking. In her passages through London, her Parisian costumes and up-to- date matter are at once the astonishment and envy of her friends. She is yet young—in the twenties —possesses a low, capable forehead, and .clear grey brown, thoughtful eyes, which, however, sparkle with a merry twinkle on the slightest provocation, The geological world awaits her next move with some curiosity and impatience.

"Madge" is the nom de plume of Mrs.liumphreys one of the most successful lady journalists, whose " Girl's Gossip," in " Truth " was among the earliest columns ever started exclusively for the feminine sex. " Madge;' though an exceedingly hard worker herself, is of opinion that the home is a woman's sphere. Mrs. Humphreys lives in Mania-vale, she :is or middle height, her hair sprinkle,' with whits, though her complexion has the rosy freshness of a girl's, and her blue eyes are very bright. " Madge's" little daughter Pearl, who is about ten years old, is to follow her mother's profession one day.

If Sir John Stainer, M.A., elects to go over to the world's Fair to judge the pianos and organs, as be has been asked to do by caule from Sir 11. Trueman Wood, there will be at leant one right man in the right place at Chicago. No one is More competent to do the work than be who wiis the organist at St: Paul's Cathedral, and in now Professor of lusic at the University of Oxford, where he livestin coin- pnrative retirement, necessitated in part ay an 4ficction of the eyes. Sir • John's first birthday occurred in London in 1840, aud seven years later lie joined the white-robed choir of the metropolitan cathedral. During the nine years lie spent there he often accompanied the service on the organ. So quick was his progresa that in 1856 he got his first appointment as organist at St. 13enedict's, Paul's 11 harf. Subsequently Magdalen College, Oxford, had his services, and'on the resignation of Sir John Goss, at St. Paul's he was selected for the post.' Ile has hardly an equal as an executant, and his church music—chaste, devotional, and full of harmony— shows the skill of the master.

Apropos of Rubinstein, the famous artist has just returned to St. Petersburg, where he will reside for the present, if not for the future. Wild horses can- not drag Rubinstein on to a concert platform, although £25,000 awaits him In America for 50 per- formances. 1 .do not think even £50,000 would tempt hid). as he has grown both shy and independ- ent in his old age. The largeat sum ever taken by, any musician at a single performance in London wad taken by Rubinstein at Sc. James's Hall, when the receipts were over £l,OOO. Paderewski, although his takings have been enormous, has never reached the figure drawn by Rubinstein.

ItnbinsWn isa great gambler, and be has been known to lose the receipts ut a week's concerts at single sitting. Years aga he put by a certain amount which he vowed, come what, might, he would 'never touch, and he bus kept his word. So when luck went against him at the curd table—and lie is dreadfully unlucky at ears—he ut•ed to get a bit, on amount from his Berlin imprez,sario.

It is a pity Mr. Monte Carlo Wells has not thought fit to give the mime of the American gentleman who advanced him the £30,000 with which lieswas enabled to break the bank. Perhaps. like Frau Zierentier's financial backers,he is dead. Some people are saying Wells' American bucker was Mr. Harry Rossenfeld, the well-known plunger. But this is a mistake. Rossenfeld, when at. Monte Carlo, played for his own hand, lie broke the bank more times than even Wells; but on the whole I fancy he left more money behind him than he took away from Edmond Blanc and Co.'s tables.

Ros..senfeld's play was quite different from that of IVells. he invariably went upon a 'single num- ber, and the number upon which he made his great coups was 17. But staking on single nutribers at roulette is simple madness unlesi .t he most extra- ordinary luck is for the moment with the staker ; in the long run even a Rothschild Doubt suczumb.

Prince henry of Battenberg is exceedingly un- lucky at games of chance. In his lieutenant's days in Berlin them was scarcely an evening Qll which he did not tempt Dame Foamiest the Union Club, and baccarat was the tickle jade that ea-wd him of his dialers. Prince henry was a very modest " punter," and a thaler at a time was about the limit of hia stakings, although he has been known to " punt" a whole fire-mark piece at one time. So unlucky was Prince Henry ti,w, on wore than one occasion "punters" have. declined to sit next to him at the table; for gamblers are slavishly suupir- stitious about lack. Since Ids *Marriage baccarat has had no fascination for Prince'lleikry.

Quince Jim.

_ Peel, core, and slice the fruit • weigh it, cover it well with water, and boil it till it becomes soft ; throwaway the water and add fresh warm water in the proportion of a pint of water to a pound of fruit ; mash the trait and the water well together as you mash potatoes, and then press it through a colardier, or, better still, a coarse wire sieve. At this stage the mixture ought to be of the consistency of .apple sauce. Then add sugar equal in quantity to the original weight of fruit; put the fruit and sugar Into a clean pan, and boil it slowly, stirring it constantly until it becomes a bright red colour and con- sistent, like corn flour about to be molted. Unless the water be added, the fruit will be found altogether tx) stiff to work with, and, if boiled too , long, the jam will become too hard for ordinary household purposes.

Marmalade, Pudding. , This pudding may be made: in ttfe following manner : —One quart of milk, four eggs, One cup of sugar, slices of stale bread buttered ; fruit marinalade, peach is best if you have it, but apple, quince, raspberry, will do if you have not. Scald the milk and pour it on the eggs; which should have been beaten light with the sugar. Return to the farina kettle and cook five minutes, but not until it thickens. Cut the bread an inch thick, pare off the crust, butter ontiodi sides, cad cover the bottom of a pudding dish with slices fitted in neatly. Spread the marmalade thick on this layer and wet with the boiling custard, waiting to see if it absorbed before put- ting another layer above it. Proceed in this order until all the materials are ut,ed up. Fit a plate or other lid upon the bake dish, and let the VI lio!e stand for half en hour to absorb the custard before it goes into the oven. Bake, covered, until the pudding is heated through, than brown nicely. Eat cold with cream. This excellent pudding may be made more elegant by whipping the whßeS of three eggs to a meringue with a tablespoonful of powdered sugar, and spreading it over the top after it begins to brown. Shut the oven door until the meringue is faintly coloured.

The Medicine chest. The following lines are said to have been written by Sidney Smith to ,a la 4 'named Howard, who had asite...l his advice as to stocking a medicine chest : With store of powered rhubarb we begin ; (To leave out powdered rhubarb were a sin), Peak mild magnesia deep within the cheat; And glittering um from Araby the Blest ; And keep, 0 lady, keep within thy reach The slimy surgeon, blood-devouring leech. Laurel-born camphor, opiate drugs prepare. They banish pain and calm consumin care. Glauber and Epsom salts their aid combine, . , Translucent streams of castor oil be thine, And gentle manna in thy bottle shine. If morbid spot of septic sore invade, By heaven-sent hark the morbid spot is Stayed When with black bile hepatic regions sell, With subtle calomel the plague expel. Anise and mint with strong 2E)lian sway, Intestine storms of flatulence allay', And ipecacuanha clears the way. Soda and potash change the humours crude, When hoven parsons swell with luscious food. I know thee well, thou a:tame:AM power, And to thee fly its that heart-rending hour When feverish patients heave their laden breath, And all is sickness, agony, and death ! Spare not in Eastern blasts when babies die The wholesome vigeur of the .Spanish fly ; From timely torture seek thy infant's rest, And spread the poison on his labouring breast. And so, tair lady, when in evil hour Less prudent mothers mourn sonic faded flower, Six Howards valiant and six Hawards fair, S ball live to love thee, and reward thy care.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
ME DEAREST NELLIE,

A material much in favour this summer for sea- side and river wear is grey flannel, which although not particularly attractive looking itself, haa really a very stylieh appearance if well made up. A good example has the moderately wide unstiffened skirt trimmed with five cross-way bands of narrow striped black and white flannel, the bodice being quite full after the manner of a sailor blouse, only that the ordinary square collar is replaced by wide double revers, the under one being of plain and the upper of striped flannel. A small tucked chemisette of white silk is shown at the throat, and the belt is of black ribbon with a jet buckle, while a bright red tie gives a pleasant touch ef colour. Pain and striped flannelette would make up cheaply and well in this style, and the latter might or course be banded with colour instead of black if preferred, but t Ile quieter mixture is nicest. I must not forget to say that brown shoes and stockings are alniest invariably worn with both this style of dress and the brown serge dresses which I have already referred to. •

Millinery forma a very expensive item in most ladies' dress allowances and this is more par- ticularly felt when colours are worn, as it is difficult to make one hat serve for several gowns. The fashions this season are extremely numerous, but tome of the most dainty I have seen were made of fancy straw trimmed with roses and other flowers.

That this is to all intents anti purposes a lace Season I have mentioned before, and now I note' that Lee insertions are being used on all kinds of dresses, hut more particularly on those of cotton. It is quite an ordinary occurrence for a simple gown to have as many as three or live rows of two-inch wide insertion run round the skirt hi hoop fashion. The same trimming is carried out on the bodice generally, with stripes of insertion forming a yoke and one or more stripes of tke seine running down the sleeves. This is a good way of altering the appearance of a last year's gown. The material is not cut away from under the insertion, and the colour shows through with very good effect. Zonaves or Figaro jackets, with or without sleeves, are much too useful to be overlooked, and in light cloths or bright velvet they are wonder- fully becoming. They should be lined with silk of the same colour as the blouse with which they are worn, these being very smart in crepe de chine or washing silk. Many have very broad revers turned well back on the shoulders.

A particularly pretty bodice is made in mauve cotton, striped with white, and sold at 24. Hid. It is arranged with a very deep shoulder frill, and Is beautituby made throughout. The bodices can be obtained in pie pink striped with whits, and also in plain zephyrs of various colours, as well as in figured and spotted cambric& Amongst this season's fashions was a beautiful toilette of mirror-grey atin, brocaded with a design of "ich dien " plumes, and embroidered most exquisitely with fine ribbon flowers, aomething like tambour work, intermixed with silver thread, spangles. pearl, and crystal beads. This fairy-like trimming as carried up two narrow panels of mauve satin, and gracefully wanders over on to the pale grey brocade in truly artistic fashion. The bodice has a deep collar of old Italian point, embroidered side-pieces, a brocade front, and crossing the bust from side to side is an original and smart bow of grey satin powdered with pearls and spangles. Another lovely confection was a robe d'interieur of ophelie Bengal satin, made in princess shape, and turned back from collar to hem with broad guipure lace and disclosing an underdress festooned with chains and rosettes of cut jet. Over the shoulders depend similar girandoles, while a draped collar and waist-belt of ophelie velvet complete a most attractive and tasteful ensemble fit for any queen,

A very taking costume was of black er4on, trimmed with two small llounces Of black satin, headed with narrow jet insertion. The bodice has trimor.;ng to correspond. It is astonishing how few wltnrn have mastered the art of walking, which, after all, is one of the best exercises in the world, and the foundation of all others. True, all who ore not absolutely crip- pled can "proceed by mans of their feet," but that is not true walking. Tee body should be held erect, shoulders down, chest extended, and the leg moved from the hip; the whole figure im- movable above this point. The Movement from the knee is the secret of nearly all bad walking, combined with the uncertain tread induced by tight boots with high which render gait uneven, and swiss the figtue in a meat ungrneelid• manner, A good trick walk should be taken every morning, wet or line. Walking, like all ether exereires, should never be carried to ex- tremes; a brisk spin will be fAr more beneficial than a tramp of many miles, resulting in utter weariness.
Yours sincerely, JENNIE •

Good Speakers Amongst Women. Amongst women whl aro good speakers, both the Princess Pf Wales and the Princess Louise are capable of saying the right thin at tlie proper moment, and the Baroness Burdett Coutts and Lady Randolph Churchill can both speak in a thoroughly earnest manner almost without preparation of any' kind. Lady Henry Somer- set, too, is often eloquent ; and amongst actresses, Miss Fanny Brough—who manifests the deepest ipterest in the welfare of her sister a etresses—can always arrest the ul :Le I,er pLuleaaivu.

div.head: IHE EVE OF TRAFALGAR.
div.p: IHE EVE OF TRAFALGAR.

Nelson, embowered down at ever-pleasant Mer- ton, making hay, watching sheep, catching trout in the winding Wandle, idolising Lady Hamilton, that beautiful but wanton woman, forgot ambition, and grew more intent on rich awnings than French canvas. One daybreak, Captain Blackwood brought word that the French had refitted at Vigo and got into Cadiz. Nelson paced the" quarter-deck "walk in the garden restlessly. Ho pretended to be indifferent, and voted a playful proverb : "Let the man trudge it, who's lost his budget." Ho was happy, and his health was better. " He wouldn't give sixpence to call th:, king his unzle." Lady Hamilton knew the heart of the brave man she loved, and pres.ed him to go. The French fleet was his property ; it was the reward of his two years' watching. He would be miserable if anyone else had it. " Nelson offer your services." The tears came into his eyes at her keroism. At half past ten that night he started in a post-chaise for London. His diary for that day lays bare his heart before us : " Fri- day night (September 13th), at half past ten," ha says, I drove from dear, dear Merton, where I left all which I hold dear in this world, to go to serve my king and country." The embarkation of Nelson at Portsmouth was a scene worthy of Grecian history. Although he tried to steal secretly to his ship, crowds collected, eager to see the face of the hero they venerated. Many of the .rugged sailors were in tears ; old men-of-war's men knelt and prayed God to bless him as he passed to the ' boat.

div.p: THE REGISTRITION OF PLUMBERS.

A bill backed by several member of Parliament, for ensuring a national system ,f registration of plumbers was considered by the House of Commons Standi Committee on Trade on Tuesday. Besides registration, the objects of the bill are stated to be the provision of a scheme for the better technical education of plumbers and a System of examination by a. -joint committee of masters and operatives. Nm-registered workmen are not to be prevented following their employment, but under the .bilf they will not be allowed to represent themselves as registered plumbers. Alter some dismis- sion the ennsizlor.tion of the bill was adjourned in order that the Local Oovetnment Board might be represented at the next sitting of the Committee.

Miss Norreys and Lord Cliilion were speaking of "Miss Myner " as they crossed the quadrangle under Gwen's amazed and yearning scrutiny.. "I am very Much disappoiliked,' the k:ast India heiress remarked. "I had hope to meet the Lady Georina's companion, Alii33• Myner—the lovelist girl, Lord Chilton, I ever beheld. But. she is too ill to appear, Lady Georgina tells inc." "Miss Myner was the heroine of the accident which happened at Beeclimont some weeks, ago, was she not?" inquired the young viscount, care- lessly, little suspecting. how deeply he was inter- ested in that "heroine."._

." Yen. She very nearly lost her life. I wish that, Lord Dark wood would procure a regular gover- ness for his daughter," said Miss Norreys. "I should like to sectqe this beautiful little Marian as my own companion. I might even be tempted to adopt her as a sister—if such a thing were possible. Ah, here we are!" _ _

, They passed in at the great arched portal, with' its double Swinging doors. Traversing a stone passage, they entered the banqueting hall, which, centuries before, had echoed to the mirth of high-born cavaliers and dames, but which for three-score years had been given over to solitude and .tourists. It was long, wide, and lofty, with groined arches overhead and magnificent carvings, the wood blackened by time to the colour of ebony. , The walls were wainscotted from floor to ceiling. The floor, hard and black, was polished to the semblance of a mirror. The gloom of the place had been lighted by the preparations for the evening's festivity. Silver sconces had been screwed to the walls, candelbra filled the mantelpieces and shelves, and these were clustered thick with tall Wax candles ready for lighting. The great yawn- ing chimneys were filled with growing plants in full flower, and down the length of the great room upon both sides, Lord :I),trkwood had caused to be placed, i nie!!y of that orange avenue in the Beeclunont eon .at ry where, last night, he had declared hislvi o Miss Norreys, a double row of orange trees, 4tll in full leafage, and • fruitage.. ' r Under the orange tree.b were seats for wallflowers and tired dancers.

The party promenaded up and down the room, and then, guided by their .host, explored the re- mainder of the ruins. They visited the chapel, the state chambers, the great drawing-room, the small dining hall, and even the kitchens and offices, leaving no closet Or chamber unexplored. They climbed the steep and narrow stairs to the upper rooms, and finally to the battlements and watch- towers, gazing ont and down tipon a fair and pleasant scene that was like one vast-park. As they returned to the lower apartments, Miss Norreys took the Lady Georgina into notice, and the girl, pleased and flattered, chattered like a magpie, telling al.out her former visit, and how she had been "so frightened" by a screech owl, or, as she believed, and should always believe, by a ghost. "Oh, but Lady Georgina," expostulated Miss Norreys, "people don't believe in ghosts in this enlightened nineteenth century. It must have been an owl you heard." . . . _

"Owls don't give such unearthly groans," cried the Lady Georgina. " Ah, that mist have been imagination." "It was not," cried the girl, energetically; "it was a cry, half groan, half shriek " The marquis drew nearer. He deemed it best to keep an eye upon his daughter, and to know what she was saying. Her lack of beauty seemed, to be equalled by her lack of sense. He heard her last words, and she stopped speaking as she caught his menacing look. Miss Norrcys saw that look also. It afforded her food for thought.

"Georgina is iineh a child, Miss Norreys," the marquis remarked, as if apologetically. "She believes in ghosts and the like; but there's time enough for her to outgrow her little superstitions —time enough to learn a little English conimon sense and wisdom. Ten years from now she will be able to hear the screech of an owl and not be frightened by it into the belief that a ghost is call- ing to her." "I have a love for an old place, grown over with ivy, given up to desolation, and clustering with old legends and superstitions," said Miss Norreys. "What scenes have transpired within these old walls during their eight hundred years of existence Men have ridden forth to battle from its gateways. In the chapel the services for the bridal and the burial have been uttered. Joy and sorrow have each been supreme here in their turn. • Women have mourned and loved here, children have waked the echoes with their glad voices. How much has happened here during eight hundred years. !" Mrs. Kenright echoed the last sentence. "I have heard that the Lords of Darkwood have been always leaders," said Miss Norreys. "They were lords of a great manor, over which they were supreme, holding in their hands the power of life and death; they were captains of a great troop; they'took prisoners in battle and consigned them to the dungeons below, leaving theni oftentimes to perish there. Men were brutal in those early days. They say, Lord Darkwood, that a skeltbn was found in one of the dungeons years ago." "That is true ! " "I have great curiosity to see, those horrible underground chambers," said the East Indian heiress. "I heard that sonic of them were hewn out. of the solid rock. Let us make a torchlight pilgrimage to the dungeons." She looked at her host with seeming carelessness, underlying which was a keen, sharp scrutiny. He turned pare; she noticed the fact. He essayed an excuse, but his daughter and his guests joined in a petition to be ellown the dungeons by torch- light. -

—"lt is not safe to go below," be stammered, the cold sweat starting on his forehead. "Why there ai'e no insecure floors down there," exclaimed Colonel Warburton. "What can render it unsafe to go below ?" "The damp, the chill, the malaria. And there are. ferocious rats---" , _

" We will defy all the horrors," interrupted Sir Willikun Ensor." Miss Norreys has set her heart on seeing the dungeons and we have all our share of curiosity." "Tourists have always been allowed to visit the dungeons," said Miss Kenright, "and no one was ever eaten by a rat or become consumptive in con- sixpence. You think ns Urn deli Cato, Lord Dark- wood, but women are hardier than you think.". Under this general battery the margnis was Corn• pencil to give in. • Yet he made still a feint of re- sistance.
"The keys are mislaid, I think," he exclaimed. "They are never required to be used and have been thrown aside."
"I know where they are 1" cried Lady Georgina. " They are in the cabinet in your library, father. There's Pietro in that room yonder. Let him go for them." Pietro advanced from an inner room. _ _ .

Lord Dark wood gave him the errand with a look of warning that included volumes of meaning. Miss Norreys caught that look also. The Maltese glided away, presently returning with a bunch of keys, which he handed to his master.

An instant's glance showed the marquis that three or four rings had been removed from the chain, and he recovered his equanimity with the discovery. "Pietro," he commanded, "let torchlights be brought." Pietro darted away again, returning with several servants bearing torchlights. "Now we will visit the underground. rooms," said the Lost. "You will find them a perfect labyrinth, KO it will be well to keep together. Miss Norreys, permit me to take you under my especial care. The stair is steep." The party, all life and merriment, descended to the dungeons. Pietro received the keys hack from his mast6r, and open Ple door of the dark cells, telling long and exciting stories about the prisoners who had suffered in them, and his master secretly resolved to bestow upon him a sum of money as a reward for his shrewdness, ready .wit, and ingeuity.

A rat went skurrying past the gronp as they listened to one of Pietro's interminable but interesting fictions. Airs. Kenright gave a shriek and clung to Lord Dark wood like a barnacle to a ship. Miss Eilsor, frightened, yet delighted with the story, clung to his lordship's remaining arm; and the Lady Georgina also crowded to him for protection, ssuail lan cursed his luck. Ji• would imit

lied i\lis Komiys to cling to him in terror, but )t)wa .m)io where in the background" with 'Lord. Chilton, he thought. • 1411; be was not. She-. was a brave and fearless woman, WO she had project in hand. She wanted, to heo,:;.,ths cry of that ghost o owl ,which had frigh;f;lll.l corgina. . So, slipping away from the group listening to Pietro's fiction connected to pass away the time, she quitted the cell; borrowed a torchlight of one of the 'servants, and sauntered away a few paee's 'as in idlest curiosity. • After' a• little, - she ran along . the corridors; turning into branch passages, and, ,when at a safe distance from her friend,-called aloud in a clear, shrill voice that waked t,lie echoes. • . .• A rat or two ran past herb But no .owl hooted; so ghostly voice cried out through the sepulchral • stillfieSs and gloom. '• She eaught np her long' robe in one hand, held her torch aloft in the other, and sped onwards, crying shrilly. Up one passage, down another. She paused now and then to beat ukon a locked- door, and then flew away as if pursued. A wild excitement possessed her. She looked back over her shoulder, fearing that Lord Darktvood was coming after her. Her eyes were wild, her face white. She ,looked as if fleeing from a ghost, rather than a person in search of one. . . At fast, panting and exhausted, she halted. Her torchlight was burning low. With a last ex- piring enemy, she gave a wild shriek. Hark! What was that? A cry, half groan, half scream, a cry as from a sepulchre, muffled, ghostly, came through the air. In the same moment she heard Lord Darkwood's voice calling her, and her torchlight died . out suddenly.
CHAPTER L. RECOGNITION

kiss Norreys was alone in the awful gloom of the subterranean passage. Her heart beat like a drum. She'panted for breath. She was horror- stricken by that muffled, far-off cry of agony, and stood as if paralyzed.

Was it some distorted echo of her own cries? Was it some Screech owl which she had disturbed in its haunts? Was it a freak of excited imagina- tion ? Hark ! It came, again I It Sounded afar-off, a wild and muffled cry, a prayer of awful agony, end- ing in a low, 'hollow groan ! What could it he?- Whence came it? From aboye? Below •!-- IL could 'not come from the. cells beside her. It seemed rather to float in the air, a spectral voice—the cry of some wandering soul flitting throuji these dim shades. , - Miss Norreys trembled like a leaf. And now again sounded Lord Darkwood's voice in the distancr, foil of alartiy awaking the echoes. Miss Normys was recalled to herself with start- ing ,Violence.

fle must not find me here !" she said tb herself. "He must not. even gums that I suspect, him !" • The sound of his voice aroused her to new life' and animation. ',With her dead torch still held • high above her head, with her eyes shining through the darkness, she 'Sprang forward, turned the nearest corner, and flitted through it second passage, another and another, in a wihl, made haste. By good fortune, more thim by conscious exer- cise of reason, she drew near to her starting-point, and to the group she had left. She saw their torchlights in the distance, heard their voices, and panned to calm herself. •I . Her heart was still beating violently; she waited until it had gain its normal pulsations ; she was wild and excited; she felt that her face might betray her, and she stood there in the deep dark- ness watching the lights, and hearing the voices, until she had grown calm and completely mistress of herself..
Then she moved forward, calling aloud to Lord Da.rkwood and the others.

They heard her voice and advanced swiftly to meet her—all save the maaguis, who was still wan- dering in remote passages in search of her. "Why, where have you been, Miss Norreys ?" exclaimed Miss Milly Kenright, speaking the question they all would have asked. We have been so alarmed about you. Lord Darkwood was sure that you were lost in these frightful cor- ridors." _ _
Miss Norreys laughed, and very naturally indeed.

"1 wenton in advance to explore the cells," she said, carelessly. "I did not care to hear those" ghostly stories which seemed to eutra,nce you all. But I find that a guide is necessary, and keys also. The_passages seem endless and the cells are all loc2ed."

She flung away her extinguished torch and glanced at her dress, which escaped injury. Nothing in her actions or manner gave the least hint of her secret experiences. She looked care- less, indifferent, untroubled, and even Pietro, who was staring at her with piercing eyes, thought with the others that her disappearance had been without object and that she had not gone far in her explorations. . _
. -- "I will tell my lord that the lady is fointi !" he exeahned. "His lordship is looking for her in great alarm." _
Torch in hana, the valet hurried in pursuit of his master. ,

"NVeren't you frightened nearly out of your senses, Miss Norrey's ?" cried the Lady Georgina. " After your light went out, I mean? And did you hear the ghost, or owl, as •father calls it ?" "I did not hear either ghost or owl, Lady Georgina," replied the East India heiress deliber- ately„ _

"-We were frighnened about you, Sicily," said Mrs. Keuright. " Yen might easily have been lost down here. And there are treacherous pitfalls in these rocky; floors. Lord Darkwood was really scared at your escapade. And as for we, I've had quite enough of -this damp, chilly, subter- ranean horror ! I shall return to civilised regions and, daylight at once. Clara, Milly, I insist upon yonr accompanying Inc. You will get your death- colds here?

"I have had enough of it also,lisaidMissNorreys. "Let us go up stairs !" The party accordingly returned to the upper rooms, and to the great banqueting hall. They were promenading here in excellent spirits, even Mrs. Keuright having recovered her usual equanimity and comfortahle warmth of body, when Lord Darkwood, followed by his valet, made his appearance.

There were traces of recent agitation in his lord- ship's face and mantle:. He had run up and down the subterranean passages in wild alarm ; he .had stopped now and then to shunt Miss Norrey's name; he had tried the doors of the cells in terror, lest one among them—and that one of great import- ance—should chance to have been left unlocked, and Miss Norreys have gained entrance to its in- terior.

But, singularly enough, he heard no cries of agony, no ghostly groans, no unlined screams or shrieks. He heard only the echoes of his ilying stops and voice. . . He traversed nearly ,all the passages and was approaching the dungeons of the far tower, when Pietro came in swift pursuit of him. He halted, hearing his servant, and was speedily informed that Miss .1-ST(n-reys was quite safe, and that she . had re• turned to her friends.

"There was no need of all this excitement on your part, signor," cried the Maltese, somewhat roughly. "It only tends to arouse comment She strolled on a little in advance, expecting you to follow her—oh, I know the arts of women, whether they be peasants or queens ! She turned into the next passage, and there her light went out. She came back as smiling and careless, looking at her dress lest by chance a drop of damp had touched it little dreaming that you had galloped off, on filisling that she had disappeared and were in pursuit of her in this quarter.' The marquis looked ashamed of his terror, which did seem really unreasonable and foolish now that he looked back upon it. "When a man has a secret, Pietro," be observed, wiping his face energetically, "he fancies that every one wholooks at him can read that. secret, or at least suspects its existence. And when Miss Norreys disappeared, I did-not stop to reason., .1 thought that, if she were to find her way to the far tower, and what if the cell-dooe should by some ill fortune have ,been left unlocked': and the very thought set me frantic !" " I see it did 1" remarked Pietro, drily. " You need more coolness, signor. The dor'''. is. locked. I have the key in my pocket. The dead eannot call out. Only your own acts lietray you. Come, let us return to your guests. Your absence will he remarked upon ! ' "Miss Norreys will attribute my anxiety to my love of her," said the marquis, with returning cool- ness. "But Pll go back. Clear out the rcst of that superfluous dirt, Pietro, and I shall he more at ease. While that remains it may betray us, and I shall be nervous and frightened at a sound." • He returned to the spot' where he had )c± • his guests. A servant was stationed there. 10/41 in- formed his lordship thnt the ,no.sts nere gone stair., and and he followed after them with a sigh of I Mist

' It Was nOw nearly dusk. The aanquetseg which. was to serve as is balk:Jou:, a'as shadows.... Theadeep, ethtle chill of 'a long saa' apartment leiaan to be perceptible, end Leal Ia wood proposed an adjoermiteut to the lai'oitablo of the castle., ' . The proposition met with favoers and the g returned to the drawintaroom,, which was brae with lights, fires, and Sowers. . At seven o'clock. dinner - was announced. • -, Lord Darkwood's cook surpassed himself ons occasion, greatly to his lordship's satisfaea The dinner was absolutely perfect. The ali, hall was - a miracle of: statelineas and grand The flowers, one soft and mellow lights, the tS. decorations—Ali were perfection. The host tart with satisfaction. All these thing i must tells'. the mind of. laliss Norreys, he thought, and nr° said to his desirableness in her estimation. After dinner they returned to the rules. The flowers had been removed' from the la° chiumeys of the ..old banqueting hall, and g!, wood:fires substituted. The 'red blaze Munn the dusky walla and floors. There were ee immense windows with arched tops, and tlain these the smooalight streamed in a Pale Between moonlight. and firelight the great halatt irradiated. A••pleasant, spies, heat was d.", throughout the apartment, and the charm 01 place VMS thus complete. The young people promenaded the ball and I, merry. A little later, a band, which had, brought: from Shrewsbury for the occasion, which was ensconced in an upper gallery go its of eight from tielow, struck up :the atesaa Strauss's favourite waltz—" The Beautiful Danube "—and to the soft, bewildering stra`lr young people swayed in the dance. Lord Darkwood claimed with aliss Nerrae' Colonel Warburton and Miss Kenright danecis gaiter. Sir William Ensor mat 111iss MillY7rj right were partners, and Lord Chilton and ~ Ensor kept time with the music. Mrs sat near one of the fires and looked on. of servants gathered outside at the windows, contemplated the scene. There were two of the dancers to whom the e: eise was absolutely repugnant, but who took Pk' in it simply for the sake of courtesy, and thee" *ere-Miss Norreys and Lord Chilton. - • The .former was occupied with her regi anxieties 'aeffprojects, and was in no humour; t dancing. • She thought frequently of airal3•°!: Ilea bailiff, apd of the telegram she had resfi upon the previous eveiabg. She thought Hindoo servant, Aga, and the mission upon she had sent him to Yorkshire. And she thous almost -continually of that strange cry ehet;i heard in the dungeon befow. It seemed , ring in her ears. It haunted her, as might' done the cry of a lost soul. Yet, oppressed by all these cares and analet-' she was smiling and courteous, a sharer ! dance, and her face was bright mei ~oyous expression, and her step light and free. Lord Chilton was heavily oppressed withan"i „ for his lost Gwen. He should have reeeival to his letter from Squire Markham, but he yet done so. Ho loathed all this gaiety, naL t lug where Gwen. might be, nor how grena poverty and loneliness, hat he here his share lasi festivity as only a true gentleman :could. peas' a nothing of his troubles to appear Mani surface, ad sacrificing himself for the pleesa,' others. At the end. of the flast dance, Miss •Ne'a• was compelled to rest. She sat dawn la' , Kenright, who remarked upon her gaiet's. her pallor two things which would lean," together.- )l The dance went on. Lord Dark woo" led ,"' 'as! Ensoi , the ot her couples exehaeging part masa 3, Chili en walked to one of the long wiettee' looked out. ore] As he did so, a slight figure which close to the window, started back abruptliaa paces into the shadow of a fir tree, amid • 'amity of which it was completely hidden. . The figure was that of Gwen, his lost lov _Hungering to see his face again, althooe% ! believed him for ever lost to her. div.head: FATAL EXPLOSION_ AT _IVIIITECROSS
div.p: FATAL EXPLOSION_ AT _IVIIITECROSS
WIR E WORKS.

An explosion took place in the Whitecross Wire Works Warrington, on Saturday morning immedi- ately after midnight, which resulted in the death of one man named Henry Kerry, aged 34 years, a puddler, and residing at 7, Glass House Row, and also injuring, two other paddlers. Kerry was following his occupation at the puddling furnace at the forge, and was in the act of making up a kcrap ball, when for some cause the furnace suddenly exploded, and a quantity of metal and debris fell upon Kerry. Thomas;Counor, and John Crouch, night mana- ger, at once went to his assistance, and the latter rendered first ald by applying bandages, and he was then taken to the Infirmary where he died at 8 o'clock a.m. Ile was very much burnt about the limbs. THE INQUEST.

The inquest on the body of Henry Kerry was held at the White Hart Inn, on Tuesday morning, by Mr. S. Briehouse, county coroner. Dr. Bowden, house surgeon at the Infirmary, said that deceased was admitted into the Infirmary at 12.30 on saturday morning, suffering frcm general burns, and died at 8 a.m. the same morning. He was conscious, but did not know how the accident happened. Witness did not think that the deceased was scalded, but burned, although he did not examine them very carefully, r.s he had to cover him up immediately. They were superficial burns. Lydia Kerry identified her husband's body. She did not see him from nine o'clock on Friday night until the morning of the inquest. The Coroner wished to knew whether H. M. Inspector of Workshops and Factories had been communicated with, and Mr. David Fanshaw, manager, who appeared for the W hitecross Company, said that he had been communicated with on Saturday. He (Mr. Fan,haw did not know why the Inspector did not appear. There Nvas no plan made out of the place where the accident occurred. The coroner suggested that the jury should visit the place in company with Mr. Fanshaw so that they could have a better idea of the whole affair. The jury and coroner accordingly adjourned to visit the place. On their return John Fisher was called to give,eyidence. He said that he was a puddler, and saw deceased working at a scrap ball half a minute before the explosion. 'The ball was inside the furnace, and ..the door was down, and deceased was working it with a bar called. a "rabble." Witness was ate it ten yards away mb-ri the explosion took place. The iurnace was blown down completely. The furnace was a steam furnace. At the bottom of the basin of the furnace there is some 1" fettle " to prevent the puddled iron from getting out. It was the puddler's duty to " fettle" the basin of the furnace. In answer to questions by the coroner and jury, witness said that the obligation was cast upon the puddler to see that the furnace was properly "fettled." It was left to his own direction. They could not always stop the cinder or slag from running out. Witness had seen it do so frequently, but never explode like on the present occasion. His opinion was that the slag had fallen through the basin of the furnace into the water and caused the explosion. Witness had known deceased two years He was an experienced puddler. There was plenty of" fettle "to be had whenever it was wanted. David Fanshaw, the manager of the forge, was the next witness. Mr. Evans, a juryman, asked him if he thought that a rush of gas through the furnace had caused the explosion. Witness did not think so. There was a large quantity of Slag in the furnace at the time of the explosion. The obligation lay upon the puddler to" fettle " the furnace. They could not delegate it to anyone else. There was no lack of " fettling." De- ceased was a good workman. His opinion as to the ex- plosion was that the furnace basin had not been pro- perly " fettled," and as the melted slag wilt attack any- thing else, on coming against the brick work it must have forced its way through soddenly. It would then get to the ashpit and steam wonld be generated, and thus cause the explosion. There was a quantity of water under the furnace and reaching to' the ashpit. The , mischief would be done as soon as the slag reached the water in the ashpit. If the furnace had been in good condition the slag could not have gone through the wall to the ashpit. Witness had known many explosions .to take place from the same cause, but none so severe as this one. The reason they had the water under the furnace was to cool the bottom. Witness had been a manager for 15 years but had nei‘er had an accident before. John Crouch, night foreman, said the deceased was an experienced puddler. He last saw him alive about five minutes befGre the explosion when he was making up a scrap ball. The furnace was repaired by bricklayers once each week, and oftener if required. His opinion was that the accident occurred from the escape of slag from the basin of the furnace. Deceased had intended to " fettle" the furnace after he had finished the scrap ball. Thomas Connor, and Samuel Wilkinson, one of the injured men also gave evidence, and the jury returned a verdict of 1' Accidental death."

div.head: WARRINGTON. LODGING•HOUSE
div.p: WARRINGTON. LODGING•HOUSE
KEEPERS FINED.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, Jeremiah Shorrocks, lodging-house keeper, 9 and 11, ShiP-yard, was charged with committing five breaches of the Common Lodging-hoeses Act, viz. : Allowing filth to remain in the rooms, having married occupants without having the beds properly secluded, dirty floors, dirty bedding, and overcrowding one house. Mr. Forshaw, solicitor appeared for the defence. Inspector Norman said the defendant was registered for two common lodging-houses, Nos. 9 and 11, Ship-yard. one was registered to accommodate 19, and the other 6. On the 4th July he visited the defend- ant's house and found it in a " state of uproar." The landlady was drunk and a lodger was trying to seed her with ale out of a glass. The bedding and the rooms were filthy. The rooms in his opinion bad not been wept for a week. The following day he again visited the house and the landlady protested that everything was all right.—lnspector Powell said he visited the defendant's house on the 4th July. He found the place very dirty. On the 11th inst. heagain visited thishouse in company with P.C. Amson. He found a married couple sleeping in a corner of one of the rooms in which there were 12 other men, and only a quilt round the bed instead of a wooden screen. At No. 11 he found that h.nise very dirty and overcrowded. The house was regis- tered for six persons and he found eight persons living there. A woman and a child were sleeping on an old squab. P.C. Mason corroborated.—Mr. Forshaw said with regard to the charge of failing to cleanse the bed- ding,he would call the Charwoman engaged,who washed sheets weekly. He admitted it was true that on the 11th July one house was overcrowded. A woman with a child came to the house at 11.30 p.m.,and begged to be taken in, and she was allowed to sleep on the sofa, for which they charged her nothing. Be thought it was far better to take the woman in, instead of allowing her to ramble about the streets. On the 11th July the screen which was formerly there was taken down,owing to the heat. Evidence in support of the defence was given by Elizabeth Burn, William Heusliall, and Mary Ann Davies. The magistrates fined defendant ss. and costa on four charges, but dismissed the one of overcrowding. Mr. Norman then applied for defendant's license to be cancelled, on the ground that he was not a suitable person to carry on a lodging-house. Mr.Forshaw opposed the application, as there had not been one tittle of evi- dence against the defendant during the two years he had held the license, and it was the very first time he had been brought before the Bench on any charge what- ever. The magistrates refused to cancel the license.— Michael Roach, 14, Stanley-st., and• Mary Galvin, 10, Friar's Green, each lodging-house keepers, were also charged with failing to remove filth from theirimuses, on the 4th inst. Inspector Powell having given evidence, the magistrates inflicted a fine of 55., including costs.

div.head: MORE ROBBERIES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MORE ROBBERIES AT WARRINGTON.

--- On Monday morning, a few minutes after two o'clock, between £l5 and £2O worth of jewellery consisting of silver necklets, alberts, and a few rings were stolen from the shop window of Mr. George Jackson, pawnbroker. 59 and 61, Church-st., Warring- ton, of which shop Mr. Calvert is manager. The thieves in order to secure the articles named, broke a plate glass ninth w, which is of considerable size and thickness, it being about seven feet long by eight feet broad, and is guarded by iron railings atß.tit a yard high. 'the crash of the glass was heard by many persons living in the vicinity, and the robbers must have immediately made a grab at what was most convenient to reach, and made good their escape. One person who lived opposite the shop distinctly saw two men, one ran up Orford-st.,and Ihe other down an entry near Mr. Jackson's yard, and this is verified by some of the jewellery which was dropped by the thieves in their hasty flight, being found in two different directi,ns. Luckily for the proprietors both the jewellery and the windows were insured.

A most daring robbery was perpetrated at the Win- wick-street Post Office, which is in the care of Mr. J. Wood, on Monday morning, which must have taken place between 10.30 and three o'clock. The money taken in the Post Office is kept in a chest of little drawers behind the counter, but they are not under lock and key, and it was found when Mr. Broadhurst, from the central Post Office in Sankev-street, came to balance up, and take the cash, that £25 in gold had been taken by someone,during the absence in the kitchen of those in charge. It is not known how the thist got behind the Counter, but, it is thought the robbery has been com- mitted by someone well acquainted with the place where the gold is kept. Information was at once con- veyed to the police. The whole of the loss is, of course, borne by Mr. Wood.

div.head: WAR RINGTON.
div.p: WAR RINGTON.
FLOWER SERVICE.

The annual flower service in connection with St. Paul's Church, was held on Sunday afternoon, when the children from St. Paul's Sunday School, arid some friends assembled in the ' church. An appropriate address was given by the vicar (Rev. H. V. Pigot). The collections were) in aid of the Sunday School. The flewers which were very plentiful were afterwards taken to the Workhouse, Fever Hospital, and the Infirmary. • CONFIRMATION AT BURTONWOOD.

The first confirmation at St. Michael's Church was held a few days ago, and it proved to be a very impressive service. The Bishop of Liverpool at the last moment had to fall back upon Bishop Royston. The candidates were with one exception from Burtonwood, and they numbered 44. The sexes on this occasion were equally divided, a somewhat strange coincidence. The Bev. Canon Penrhyn accompanied the Bishop, and acted as his chaplain. The candidates, some of whom had been under instruction for upwards of a year, had been care- fully prepared by the Vicar. The Bishop expressed his pleasure at the reverence displayed by the candidates throughout the service. The newly-confirmed subse- quently made their first communion, when there were 61 communicants.

div.head: P.S.A., AT WYCLIFFE.
div.p: THE P.S.A., AT WYCLIFFE.

There was a good attendance at the P.S.A. meeting in Wycliffe Church on t'unday. Nine new members were enrolled which brings the membership total to 668. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Rigby, of Frodshatn, who delivered a short address. Mr. Whisque, of Manchester, was the speaker for the afternoon, and he based his remarks upon the text " It doth not yet appear what we shall be." Mr. G. H. Yonge was the soloist, and he sang two solos fer which he received loud applause. The Rev. John Yonc,e, Mr. John Porritt, and Mr. George Brown also addressed the meeting. It was decided to contribute the benevolent fund money collected on Sun- day next tof the relief fund of the recent Thornhill colliery disaster. THE RISFIOP OF LIVERPOOL AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

There was an unusually large congregation on Sunday evening at the Warrington Parish Church to hear the Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Ryle) preach. His lordship took as his text 2nd Timothy 4,2. "Preach the Word." He remarked that the text contained a very great and solemn command. There was no doubt this epistle was one of the last St. Paul ever wrote. He wrote as an old —in fact, as a dying man. "Preach the Word" 'here almost the last words he had uttered. It was a strange thing how the ruling passion came out strong in death. He had preached under many trials and persecutions. but this did not prevent h'm from carrying on the work he had taken in hand. He went on preaching to the , last. This was a great lesson for all who were Christ's ministers. They were not to ;give up and think that preaching was of no use. The work they did was the most useful work that could be done. Years ago men used to say they did not want long sermons, or, in fact, any sermons at all. He had lived to see a change in this respect come over men's opinions. It tended to prove that they were going back to the custom of Apos- tolic times. He was glad to see that they were going to have open air services in that parish. They were held in other places in their diocese, and they were most use- ful in getting hold of the attention of men and women, and the first step in leading many to the Church. Men might despise it for a time, but depend upon it, this preaching did far more good than people supposed. People might laugh, and sneer, and scoff, and go away, but they often remembered what wai'hpoken. His lord- ship concluded by exhorting his congregation to use every opportunity of persuading those who were indifferent to attend the House of God, in order that they might be benefited by hearing preached the Word of God.

div.head: BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The chapel anniversary services at Bewsey-rosd Wes- leyan Chapel were held on Sunday,when the preacher in the morning and evening was the Rev. Thomas Rippon. of Douglas, Isle of Mani and formerly of the Warrington circuit. There was a capital attendance both morning and evening, and the rev, gentleman preached two ex- cellent sermons, the text f,,r the evening being St. John 9,25. "He answered and said : Whet her he be a sin- ner or know, I know not. One thing I know, whereas I was blind now I see." He said that the scene between Jesus and the blind man was not only 'remarkable for its self-evident truthfulness,butalso for its dramatic interest. The retorts of the blind man were very caustic. The story was the conversion of this poor man, all proved it to be for the book of real life and told by an eyewitness. Mr. Rippon then went on to picture the scene of the miracle, and said that what the world wanted to-day was testimony to Christ like the blind man's. He con- cluded with an earnest appeal to the congregation to bear testimony for Christ, and to further His cause.

The services were continued on Monday when a large number pf persons assembled to hear a lecture by Mr. John Chatnpness on "A few leaves from the diary of an Evangelist." Mr. John Bennett, of Bewsey Hall, oc- cupied the chair and there were also on the platform the Revs. J.Kirtlan, and T.Ross and Mr.J.Champness. The meeting was opened by singing and prayer after which the Bev. J. Kirtlan in introducing the chairman ex- pressed his pleasure that his (the chairman's) son was appointed connexional evangelist by the stationing com- mittee of the Wesleyan conference. The chairman who made a very amusing speech expressed his sympathy with evangelistic work. He would like to see every village in England visited by evangelists. The Rev. Thomas Champness of Rochdale, brother of the lecturer had 140 evangelists, but there was work for even more than that number. He had very great pleasure in call- ing upon the lecturer to give his lecture.—Mr. J. Champ- ness, at once put his audience in a good humour by ! telling a few amusing anecdotes, and then proceeded to give an account of his evangelistic work, in which i he had visited the greater part of England. He told how 1 he was called at almost a moment's notice to undertake some mission services at Hadfield in the Glossop circuit from which time he has been at the work almost re- peatedly. He laid great stress upon personal visitation at the places where he held his mission, and did not even miss public-houses, and told several anecdotes to illus- trate the good resulting from such work. The lecturer has all the humour of his brother, the Rev. Thomas Champness and there were frequent outbursts of laughter and applause, at his comical sallies. After the lecture a hearty vote of thanks was carried on the motion of Mr. J. W. Hayward, J.P., seconded by Mr. Davey, who each mentioned the willingness with which Mr. cite mpness responded to their invitation. Mr. Champness briefly replied and promised to come again on the next anniversary services.

div.head: SIAMESE QUESTION.
div.p: THE SIAMESE QUESTION.

THREATENED SERIOUS COMPLICATION. 1 , The Siamese question is engrossing attention in France. M. Develle, the Foreign Minister. says that France would maintain her rights, and he believed that Siam would give way. From Bangkok there are reports that the King contemplates leaving the capital,and that much alarm is created by the aggressive attitude of the French captains in the river, who are constantly " beat- ing to quarters" and otherwise bringing " pressure " to bear on the Siamese. Two very important reports, if true, reach us simultaneously from Paris and Tientsin. The one is that Russia has promised to support the French " at all pints" in the Siamese question, and the other that China has determined to support Siam. A report was current in London on Thursday night that the Cabi- net had given Lord Dufferin special instructions, and that important despatches has been telegraphed to the commander-in-chiaf on the China station.

div.head: AFFAIRS OF THE LIBERATOR
div.p: THE AFFAIRS OF THE LIBERATOR
SOCIETY.

When the investigation into the affairs of the Lands Allotment Company was resumed at the London Bank- ruptcy Court on Thursday,the Official Receiver informed the Registrar in reference to the latter's remarks about the absence of Jabez Balfour, that Balfour left England prior to the winding up order. The Board of Trade had taken every step to effect his arrest, and the foreign office had been in communication with the Argentine Government with a view to securing the fugitive's extra- dition. He mentioned these facts to show that his department was blameless in the matter. The Exchange Telegraph Company says it is reported in a well informed quarter that Detective Inspector Littlechild, formerly of Scotland Yard, has recently sailed for Buenos Ayres, on behalf of a firm of solicitors whose clients are largely interested in the Balfour group of companies. It is stated Mr. Littlechild hopes to obtain from Jabez Spencer Balfour such information as may complete the evidence already taken in bankruptcy and facilitate the realisation of assets.

div.head: INT.ERESTIN G FACTS.
div.p: INT.ERESTIN G FACTS.

As a preparation for the many changes incident to. the passing of the Parish council Bill, a return , has been published by authority of Parliament, giv- ing the number of parishes and parts of parishes in each Administrative County, County Borough, and Rural Sanitary District of England and Wales with their respective populations, from which we extract the following as bearing on this district and county. In the auministrative county of Chester there are 483 whole and 9 parts of parishes, and of these no less than 232 parishes, or nearly one half,hay.e a population of less than 300 each. In the Altrincham rural sanitary dis- trict there are 32 whole parishes and one part of a parish, 11 of which have a population of less than 300 each. The Ashton-under-Lyne Rural Sanitary Authority con- sists of two whole parishes, and one part of a parish be- longing to the county of Chester,and one part of a parish belonging to the county of Lancaster, the two county of Chester parishes, having a population of lass than 300 each. The rural sanitary district of Birkenhead consists of two whole parishes both of which have a less popula- tion than 300. In the Chester rural sanitary district, there are 44 whole parishes and one part ot a parish ; of this number 37 parishes have a population of less than 300 each. The Congleton rural sanitary district Con- tains 29 whole parishes 14 of which have a It-es popula- tion than 300 each. One Cheshire parish having a less population than 300 is situate in the Drayton Rural sanitary district, a district which consists of parishes in the three counties of Salop, Stafford and Chester. The Hayfield rural sanitary district also contains parishes in the two counties of Derby and Chester, but in this case the county of Chester parish (Disley) contains a popula- tion of nearly 20,000. The Macclesfield rural sanitary district contains 34 whole and 4 pai ts of parishes' 13 of which have a population pf under 300 each. Nantwich rural sanitary district consists of 68 whole parishes, 41 of which have a less population than 300 each. The rural sanitary district of Northwich contains 33 whole and 5 parts of parishes, 14 of which have a population of less than 300 each. The rural sanitary district of Runcorn consists of 38 whole parishes, 15 having a less population than 300 each. Stockport rural sanitary district contains whole and 2 parts of parishes, only one having a popula- tion of less than 300. The Tarvin rural sanitary district consists of 56 whole parishes, 41 having a less popula- tion than 300 each. There are 2 whole .parishes and 1 patt of a parish In the Warrington rural sanitary dis- trict, viz. :—Grappenhall, Latchtord, and Thelwall, tint all of these have populations of over 300. The Whit,- church rural sanitary district consists of parishes in the three counties of Chester, Salop, and Flint, 22 being Chester parishes,l7 having a population of less than 300. Ile Wirral mai sanitary district consists of 35 whole parishes and one part of a parish, 20 of which have a population of. less than 300 each. The rural sanitary district of Wrexham also consists of parishes in the three counties of Denbigh,Flint,and Chester,two whole parishes and one part of a parish being in the county of Chester, and having a population of less than 300 each. The great change that is proposed to be effected will thus be at once seen on reading clause 4 of section 1 of the Parish Councils Bill, which reads " A rural parish with a less population than three hundred shall, as soon as practicable, be grouped for the purposes of this Act with some other parish, so that the population of the groups shall not be less than three hundred, and every such group of parishes shall for the purposes of this Act form a parish with a parish meeting and council." The practical effect of this will be the grouping of thes?i small parishes into areas, sufficiently large as to admit of responsible and independent self-government. The aggregating Of these small parishes into suitable areas is to be the immediate work of the County Council under the provision of Section 30, but if from any cause the county has not so grouped them within twelve months after the passing of the Act, the Local Government Board will forthwith do so on their own initiative.

As the Parish Councils Bill is to be one of the Govern- ment measures of the autumn session and seeing that it is but the promised completion of the Local Government Act of 1888, passed under the regime of the late govern- ment, we may reasonably hope to see it placed on the statute book during the present year. The County Councils will thus have plenty of additional work to occupy their time and energies ; the dream of the villagers and rural labourers is within measurable distance.

div.head: RUNCORN SHIPPING CASE.
div.p: A RUNCORN SHIPPING CASE.

In the Liverpool County Court, on Friday last week, before his honour Judge Shand, an action was brought under the Admiralty jurisdiction of the court by the owners of the flat Albion (Ir. F. J. Abbot of Hooton) to recover from the owners of the steamship Hebe (Mr. W. Rowlands of Run- corn), damages for injuries through a collision on the early morning of the 26th January last in the Upper Mersey. Mr. W. F. Taylor (instructed by Messrs. Forshaw and Hawkins) appeared for the the plaintiffs, and Mi. A. G. Steel (instructed by Messrs. Bateson and CO.) for the defendants. It ap- peared that the Hebe having mitered the Mersey from Barrow the previous night, anchored in the river off Bromborough. The steamtug Earl of Ellesmere was tak- ing two flats, One of which was the Albion, from Prince's Dock to the Ship Canal,when at about three in the morn- ing she had Occasion to cross the bows of the Hebe, and in doing so the Albion ran foul of the Hebe's bows and , / sustained such injuries that she had to be beached. The ' plaintiff's case was that the Hebe's anchor lights were not properly burning,the forward light being ont.and the after one so dim that it could not be seen until they were only a few yards away.—For the defence it was sub- mitted that the people on the tug and flats had not kept a proper lookout, that the Hebe's lights were burning properly, and that the shock of the collision caused the forward light, in which mineral oil was being burnt, to go out. Witnesses from an adjoining Vessel proved the fact of the sudden going out of the light in question just an instant before-they heard the crash of the colli- sion. Experts also stated that lamps burning mineral oils were liable to go out on a sudden jerk or shock.— His Honour held that the men on the tug and flats had not kept a good look out, and added that there was no evidence upon which he could find, as against the affirmative evidence given, that the Hebe's lights were not properly burning. He therefore found the Earl of I Ellesmere alone to blame.

div.head: FROM DOCK LABOURER TO RAILWAY KING.
div.p: FROM DOCK LABOURER TO RAILWAY KING.
A LUCKY CANUCIC.

The Canadians are says U. N. Clesam in the "Sun," very proud, and justly so, of their great trans-continental railway, for the Canadian Pacific, linking the Atlantic and Pacific, is said ;o be the longest railwvy in the world under one manage- ment. But whenever this claim is urged by a loyal citizen of the Dominion within hearing of an aggressive Yankee, the latter is certain to retort, "But you had to get one of us to run it for you," a statement founded on sold fact, for Mr. Van Horne, its manager, was born in the United States. The opening last month of the Great Northern Railway, the latest and most northerly of the trans-continental railways in the United States, has furnished the Canadians with a reply to the Yankee boast, for Mr. James J. Hill, President of the "Great Northern," is a Canuck, and his magnificent work in developing from the old Manitoba Railway system this neW line froin Lake Superior to the Pacific coast places him at the very head of the railway kings of the world.

div.head: CLOCKWORK EN:AD.
div.p: A CLOCKWORK EN:AD.

_ Me. Hill s a man with a history, as anyone would sus- pect, after a glimpse of his big head, his lion face, his long hair and grizzled whiskers ; power is written in every line and feature, and Nature has written facts, not fiction, in this case. But let me tell you his story. "That boy, Hill, has got some big wheels in his head, and mark me, the world will hear them ' hum ' some day." These words were spdlten 40 years ago by Com- modore Kittson, at that time the largest Indian trader of the West ; and they were spoken of a young Canadian boy who was carrying wood and freight from the steamboat landing, on board a riier boat, loading for" down the river," at St. Paul, Minnesota, then a cluster of log cabins, with a population of less than 500 souls. There is a wide stretch of "open country" be- tween the penniless wharf labourer of 1853, and the millionaire Railway King of 1893, and thig is how Jim Hill covered it.

div.head: GOES TO WORK IN TEE DOCKS.
div.p: GOES TO WORK IN TEE DOCKS.

I When Hill arrived at St. l'aul'aliii-r;t-tried to get a clerkship,and failed, his money soon became exhausted, but,fortunately, not his pluck, for giving over his search I for "genteel work" he applied for, and secured the position of "Roustabout," or freight handler at the steamboat landing. And very hard work this proved, but while it bruised his hands it brightened his eyes, opening them to the chance of profit in the carrying trade of the western waterways. At this time the Red River of the North was the easie;t means of communica- tion between the Indian trade and his base of supply, and the small fleet of fiat-bottomed boats plying up and down the Red River were reaping a golden harvest; for they monopolised the trade, and charged extortionate rates. Young Hill noted all this, and kid his plans. He worked hard, saved every penny he could, and at last accumulated about £5O; then he hunted up a brother Canuck.

CONCERNING THE OPPOSITION. The happy possessors of an equal sum formed a part- nership and bought a flat boat, and with this modern equipment, started in to do battle with the old company To the casual observer this would appear a very foolish move, but Hill was not acting blindly ; he wrote long and glowing accounts to newspapers in the east of the great Red River traffic ; then he offered to carry freights for one half the old charges. This attack disconcerted the enemy. They did not want to have a rival line established with Eastern capital, neither did they wish their customers to he educated to low freight rates. They saw Hill meant fight, and knew how to fight. They took him into the company, and so gave him the first big lift on the way to power and fortune. After some years of money-making on the river, Hill was " long- headed "enough to realise that railways were destined to kill the steam boat business, and so without giv- ing any reason to his partner, he sold out.

Buys A EnOKEN-DOWN RAILROAD. NOW, When this young Napoleon of finance came to examine the field closely, he discovered that a railway, called the Minnesota and Pacific, and built, so far, with Dutch capital, possessed a most liberal charter, and a land grant, in size, equal to an empire. The property , had bean expensively constructed, badly managed, and the treasury was empty. Hill saw Ids opportunity, and was quick to embrace it. But first of all he had to secure additional capital. The old trapper Kittson was approached, and this man, having a lively recollection of how the young Canuck had beaten the river mono- poly, offered to advance £lOO,OOO. Still even this sum was not enough, and together Hill and Kittson visited Montreal where, through the influence of the old trap- per, they secured another £lOO,OOO. Then an agent was quietly sent over sea to Amsterdam, and the bonds of the railway company bought up, some as low as 15 per cent, of their par value. Holding now, a majority of First Mortgage Bonds"; the mortgage was fore c/osed,the road bought in by Hill and Kittson, and the Manitoba Railway Company took over the property.

div.head: SHAKING OUT KITTSON.
div.p: SHAKING OUT KITTSON.

At last in full possession of a tine railway property, Mr. Hill decided that what was good for two would be better still for one, and hence his determination to get rid of his partner. And this -vas neither a long nor a difficult piece of work. A p3licy was inaugurated of building branch lines, this plan soon exhausted the earn- ings of the road and piled up an immense debt. liittson, an old man, and a very timid operator, took fright, and sold out at a very moderate figure to his aggressive partner. After this transfer of ownership the policy of the railway changed, moderated considerably, and a special dividend of 45 per cent, was declared on the shares now chiefly held by Mr. Hill. • From that day to this Mr. Hill's fortune has increased at a marvellous rate, for the Red River Valley' in which his land grant was , largely situated, proved the finest wheat land in the United States. while the inrush of population to settle up the New North-West taxed the equipment of his rail- way to the utmost. To-day he is stated to possess a fortune of £15,000,000.

div.head: HIS LOVE STORY.
div.p: HIS LOVE STORY.

The &tint side of Mr. Hill's life is almost RR unique as its commercial. Forty years AV the poor freight hand- ler met a pretty girl at a country dance; it WoiS a case of love at first sight. Unfortunately, the girl lived at home and this home was 20 miles from St. Paul's. Jim Hill had neither time nor money to do his courting at this distance, hut the lovers solved the problems o f ways and means—lovers generally do. The girl came into St. Paul's' and to support herself, acted as waitress in the only hotel in the town. When Hill could afford it, he sent his prospective wife away to an eastern boarding- school, and two years later married her. To-day this one-timed farmer lassie presides over a home which cost to build £150,000. Among other jewels she possesses an emerald necklace valued at £12,000. She is loved and respected by all who know her, and it is said that over £lO,OOO a year is distributed by her hand to the poor to her city and State. From the windows of Mr. Hill's new home he can look down on the old wharf where 40 years ago, he arrived a penniless roristabout. while his better-half can see from the same window, the hotel, where in the far away past she was woed and won by her " hustling " sweetheart Jim Hill. They were paor and happy then ; they are rich and happy now ; for wealth, while it has changed their surrounding, has left their breasts unchilled.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE IN GOOD SPIRITS.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE IN GOOD SPIRITS.

A story is being told in the House which well represent Mr. Gladstone's exuberant buoyancy since the crisis cf the Horne Rule fateful debate was passed After the Prime Minister - had voted in the division on Clause 9 Mr. Majorihanks cameup to him and said, " I think I can find a pair for you, Mr. Gladstone,if you would like to go home now." A pair! said Mr. Gladstone, " find me two pairs, and I may. I feel equal to any two Tories to-night."

div.head: BULLDOG.
div.p: BULLDOG.

Baseldine, champion bulldog of the world, winner of the fifty-two guinea championship vase at Preston this year, and owned by Mr. Barber, of Hyde, died suddenly on Thursday morning in the railway train near Grimsby, whilst being taken bv his owner for exhibition at Grims- by. The dog was valued at £5,000, and the owner states that there was no apparent cause for its sudden decease.

div.head: ANGLING AND HOMING SOCIETIES.
div.p: ANGLING AND HOMING SOCIETIES.

A deputation from the St. Helena Angling Asso- ciation waited upon the Parke Committee on Wed- nesday afternoon, and appealed for permission to angle in the Corporation Reservoir, in the new Taylor Park. They presented a strong casq,which the committee evidently recognised, and the matter will he fully dis- cussed at a special meeting to consider the new by-laws —The St. Helena Homing Society held the first training staee for young birds on Wednesday, liberating 130 at Wellington, Salop. A good number arrived home with- in two hours.
