div.head: 000 D TEMPLAILS,
div.p: THE 000 D TEMPLAILS,

At the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening the weekly session of the Earlestown Hope Lodge of Good Temp!ars was held. Bro. E. Newman, CT., presided, and there was a good attendance. The members of the Juvenile Temple provided the evening's entertainment, and gave a pleasing selec- tion cf songs, recitations, &c., in a creditable man- ner. Addressee were delivered by Bros. Clarke, Blair, and Vi arburton. A vote of thanks was accorded to the juveniles for their visit and enter- tainment, and before leaving the room they were supplied with refreshments. Amongst other busi- ness which was afterwards transacted it was resolved to have the annual picnic to Frodsham on Saturday, August sth. After singing several melodies the meeting was brought to a close. GOLBOBNE WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. On Saturday evening the opening services iu con- nection with the new Welsh Congregatidnal Church Golborne, were commenced, Mr. W. Roberts, of Liverpool, and the Rev. R. Roberts, of Manchester, preached. On Sunday morning an ordination ser- vice was held, at which Mr. W. Roberts was or- dained pastor of the church • the officiating minis- ters being the Rev. R. lieinid Jones, of Bootle, and the Rev. P. Price. of Trefrew. In the afternoon an English service was held, conducted by the Rev. P. Price, and in the evening the same clergyman, along with the her. R. Deiniol Jones, officiated, the service being in Welsh. On Monday evening the services were continued, the Rev. James Hall, of Liverpool, conducting the service in English. The meetings have been held every night this week, and will terminate next Sunday. DISTRICT SCHOOL DRAWING Ex MINATION. The prizes won in the drawing examination made by Captain Royse, ILE., in May last, at the district school have been distributed. All children who had attended school without being once absent dur- ing the year received a prize and in each class in addition prizes were given for the various subjects taught. Two speeial prizes— a writing desk and a beautiful album—offered by Dr. Handysiae wet won by William Savage and Jane Dollen. Mr' Molyneaux kindly sent buns and nuts for the 650 children present. Miss Taylor, who hes been at the school 21 years and has earned her parchment, was presented by her colleagues with a handsome gold brooch as a token of their esteem on her leaving the school, to assume the position of head mistress. The managers have received the highest mark" Ex- cellent "for the work done.

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL GALA.
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOOL GALA.

The scholars of the Church Association Sunday Schools had their annual gala on Saturday, and as the elements were propitious and other essentials to the treat were favourable, the scholars enjoyed themselves considerably. Including the young mid old scholars, there were 500 supplied with tea. The following ladies presided over the tables, viz., Mrs. C. Hodgkinson, Mrs. Wood, Mrs. Speakman, Mrs. Turton, Mrs. lligson, Mrs. Naylor, Mrs. Byrom, Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. Bradburn, Miss Edgar, Miss Stubbs, and Miss Sullivan. After tea a possession was formed, and, headed by the School band, under the leadership of Bandmaster Steveuson,they proceeded to the residence of Mr. W. Balharry, The Beeches, Newton-road, where the usual out-door games were freely indultzed in until nine o'clock, when the entire company assembled in Mr. Balharry's yard and,accompanied by the band, sang the appropriate evening hymn "Glory to Thee, my God, this night." Hinging cheers were next given for Mr. and Mrs. Balharry, after which the procession was re-formed and proceeded back to the school, where all were dismissed.

div.head: LUNATIC'S MAINTENANCE.
div.p: A LUNATIC'S MAINTENANCE.

Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, at the Warrington COunty Police Court on Wednesday appeared on be- half of Dr. Street, of the Haydock.Asylum to apply for a maintenance order upon the Birkenhead Union for the keep of a lunatic for 56 weeks. He said that the lunatic was an American named Mr. Van Nor- den who had come over to England and married an English lady. They lived at 8 Belmont Terrace, New Brighton, but shortly afterwards lie became insane, and was sent to the asylum at Haydock on August 2Gth, 1880. The wife paid towards his maintenance more or less regularly until March 50, 1802. At that time payments ceased, and his wife said she could not afford to pay any longer, as she had to maintain herself. Nothing was done until April 15th, 1893, when he was removed to the county asylum at Chester. Dr. Street now applied for an order against the Birkenhead Union in which New Brighton is situated.—Dr. Street gave evidence in support of Mr. Davies' statement, and said that he applied for £1 per week from the time the payments ceased until the time the patient was taken away, which would amount to ..£59. The magistrates granted the application,

div.head: PERFECT THRIFT BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: PERFECT THRIFT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of tie members of this society was held in St. John's schoolroom, Earles- town, on Thursday evening week. The Rev. E. W. Whittenbury-Kaye presided. Mr. T.Latimer, secre- tary,read the report, which stated that the directors took the opportunity to express their gratification at the success obtained by the society during the first year's working, and their confidence in the system upon which it was founded. During the year six appropriations had taken place, amounting to £OOO. Three of these appropriations amounting to .C3OO were purchased by the society for £2l, .Cl5O of which was sold to a member at a deferred pre- mium of .C6O. The remaining £l5O when sold would give a lArge profit. One appronriation of .£lOO, obtained by ballot,was readily sold for a good premium, leaving a large profit to the original ' holder. The year's accounts showed a balance against the funds of .E 3 Is. 7d., but taking into ac- lount that the whole of the formation expenses were included therein, the prospect of a large pro- fit on the second year's workings were very bright. The directors bad made an arrangement whereby forty members had been admitted from Runcorn. The members now numbered 260. The report was adopted. . The financial statement showed

.. the amount of the receipts to be .£440. 10e. 101., and the expenditure was £l3B 17s. sd. The liabilities amounted to £3BO is. The following retiring directors were re-elected by ballot for two veers :—Messrs. George Clarke, Earlestown ; Wm. Kay, Golhorne; Wm. McCawley, Earlestown ; and 11. R. Toone, Runcorn. Messrs. W. Horsley and W.ll.llindley were re-elected auditors of the society for the ensuing year. SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT. A pleasant treat was enjoyed by the scholars of St. John's Sunday school on Wednesday, when 150 of them visited Winwick Hall. The occasion was the annual school treat. The party were accom- panied by the vicar the Rev. J. Carson, Mrs. Carson and the Misses Carson, and Mrs. ilolyneux (lady superintendent) and Miss Knowles, in addition to the teachers. flames of a • varied character were indulged in during the day in the ground*, where tea was also provided. At an early hour in the evening the party walked back in procession to the schools, where they were dismissed.

THE ELECTION OF COMMISSIONF.IIS. The election of Oree commissioners for Newton and Earlestown district Board of Commissioners will take place on Wednesday next. The thrPe members who retire by rotation are Messrs. T. Ormond, E. T. Evans, and J. McMahon. All three gentlemen have again been nominated and the following gentlemen have also been nominated :- 1 Mr. James Smith, Brookside ; Mr. Robert Stewart, High-street, Newton ; and Mr. John Simpson, high- street, Newton. There will be three polling stations opened, one at Wargrave School, at the Town Hall, Newton, and in Ettrle.town, probably in St. John's School, but the place has not yet been chosen. Mr. Emmett, chairman of the Board, will net as returning officer and the following are the presiding officers ;—Mr. Coliingwood, Wargrave school ; Mr. G. Ratcliffe, Earlestown ; and Mr. T. P. Gillespie, .Newton Town liall. The address of the three retiring inembersMessis. Ormond, McMahon' and Evans,will be found in out advertising columns

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

TRIC CONGREGATIONAL PASTORATH Mr. M. F. Pi rs M.A., of Edinburgh Theological Callegedias d cided to accept the assistant pastorship of Dr. Mackennars church at Bowden for twelve months. Mr. Peterson will preach at St. Helens on Sunday, but not as a candidate for the vacant vistorate.

THE BOOKS EXHIBITION. At the meeting of the St. Helens Free Library Com- mittee On Wednesday.Mr.A.Lancaster reported the atten- dance of the 13o)ks Exnibition in Victoria Park for the saleotal fpnarstt or I ffeo ;12:5(w)c months hg had e s3b,eBheoansd. been 19n1 aldn6et lohis .et btu:de including itnbhciee- tion closes this week. ELEMENTARY SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. Mr. T. Dtlf tou.superintendent.reported to the monthly meeting of the St. Helons School Attendance Committee on Wednesday,that during the past month, 1,953 irregu- lar scho'ar's had been reported, eat] the cames had been investigeed by the sub-committee. On the rods there ' were 14,944 scholars, exclusiveof half-timers, and the average a tt-dAnee was 12,455, giving an all roued per centage of 83, against 84 in the previous month. Sr. HELENS CORPORATION BILL. This Bill was to have come on Thursday before Um Select Committee of the House of Lords, over which the Earl of Jersey presides. The opposition was, however, withdrawn, and the Bill will accordingly go before Lord Morley's committee as an unopposed measure. The ob- ject of the Bill is to extend the borough of St. Helens ; to consolidate the townships within the borough ; to dis- solve the Burial Board ; and to maim better provisions for the health, local government, and improvement of the borough, and for other purposes.

- BOLLINFARE CIIIIRCIT. The annual school sermons were preached at flollinfare Church on Sunday. In the morning the Vicar,the Rev.G. F.Roberts,conducted the service. The anthem was taken from Rey. Vii, 1317. Special hymns were sung by the cht.ir. In the evening there was a good congregation, the preacher being the Rev. H. Vernon Pit, M.A., vicar .f St. Paul's, Warrington. The anthems. taken from Ezek. xxxiv. 14-15 and Psalm xxiv. 343-10 were well sung by the choir, the bass solo being effectively taken by Mr. Lythgae. Mr. Crossley presided in an able manner at the organ. The collections were in aid of the schools.

OPENING OF A :gm LABOUR CLUB. On Sunday afternoon a new labour club.house, in connection with the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, was opened at St. Helens, the Peel Arms, which was clo3ed by the magistrates about four years ago. having been secured for that purpose. There are large billiard rooms, five other rooms and refreshment bar, giving accommodation for 200 men. Mr. Peter John King, who presided, said he was determined to fight in the interest of labour and labour alone, as neither the Liberal nor Tory parties had the labour interest at heart. He urged those present to be true to labour.—Mr. Edward Wflugh and Mr. G. J. Lynskey also addressed the meeting. THE 6WANDERINGS OF ST. HELENS CITIT.DREN. On Saturday afternoon John Whittle, aged seven years, of 5, York-place, and Arthur Twist, aged six years, of 23, Cooper-st., St. Helens, strayed from their homes and were missing until Sunday. The children had followed the Volunteers to the railway station, and when returning took the wroeg road and went towards llaydock. They were picked up outside Ashton, a dis- tance of seven and a half or eight miles from St. Helens, and only being able to give their names, their homes could not be ascertained. On Sunday the St. Helens town crier (George Kirk) was engaged,and he succeeded in tracing the children to Ashton. where they had been made very comfortable at a wayside cottager SERIOUS ACCIDENT. On Monday afternoon a serious accident happened at the Globe Works (St. Helens) of the Hilited Alkali Com- pany. Thomas I,9ckenby, aged thirty-six, of Traverse. street, was, with other workmen, setting bricks, which are made from purple ore, in the kiln. About twenty- five tons had been placed in a large kiln. The ore prior Pa being burnt is of a very friable nature, and when Lockenby was returning out .f the kiln about four or five tons of the bricks collapsed and partially buried him. His left lez was broken and lie received serious injuries to his head and arms. He was removed to the Pr4vidence Hospital and attmded by Dr. Knowles.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE: A REMARKABLE CASE. At St. Helens on Tuesday, before Alderman M'Bryde, Mr. W. J. Thomson, and Mr. T. Glover, a vvorking, man named Thomas Marsh, of Back-lane, upon whom a dis- tress warrant had been served for non-payment of a fine under the Reueation Ad, appeared in court, and said he had not mite- lent goods to meet the fine, and preferred to go to prison for the seven days. He said it was a .confounded shame that he was fined at all, as his girl was fourte(m years of age, and had been in the fifth and sixth standards,—Mrs. Marsh created a scene in court by her volubility in defence if her hushand.—The Clerk : Yi-u are talking nonsense.—Mrs. Mitch: I am not talk- ing nonsense.—Tiv• Clerk : This girl is over thirteen, and under fourteen, and under the Act an attendance order was made. Under that order Marsh is liable to be fined until the girl is fourreen.years old. He was fined, and you (the bench) have get to enforce that fine.—The magistrates granted a committal, and NI2 rsh was ; removed to the cells. ALLEGF.D THEFT OF A WIFE'S WATCH. At St. 11-lens, on Thursday, before Alderman Harrison and Mr. Martin, a working man named William Brown, of 19, Ardwick-street, Parr, was charged with having stolen a silver watch, value £4, the property of his wife The circumstances as narrated by Chief Constable Wood were peculiar. The prisoner had been married to prosecutrix five or six years. and four years ago he was committed for three months for having committed an avgravated assault upon his wife. A jiadicid separation was also made. After he came out of prison he lived with her for about a. fortnight and then went away. Four months ago he again went to the house, and the watch was hanging over the fire-place. On the follow- ing day it was missed, and Mrs. Brown gave informa- tion to the police. Police-constable Hughes arrested him yesterday.end he said," I did get it and sold it to a barman for .6:."—Margaret Elliott, his stepdaughter, said her mother was very ill and unable to appear.—The prisoner was rem nded. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE : ALLEGED PERSECUTION. During the hearing of a num ner of sclipol eases at St. Helens on Friday, Mr. Dromg,ools, one of the magistrates spoke in strong terms of the case of Thomas Antrobus, who had been summoned in respect of a girl between thirteen and fourteen years of age. The mother said the girl had a bad ear every spring, end she tried to get her into a school, hut could not. Mr. Droingoole thought the mother had made tan honest attempt to get the girl to school, and asked, "Is it worth while to continue . . .

this persecution ?"' Superintendent Dutton said he could not withdraw the case. Mr. Dromgoole :It will be dismissed then.—ln a subsequent case, where a com- mittal was asked for, Ihe superintendent said he c mid not say that the father had definite knowledge that an order had been made on him. Mr. Droungemle thought the man knew nothing about the proceedings, and it was a hardship to commit him if he had no definite . knowledge. Ile wonld decline to sign such committals. Mr, 'l'. Glover also declined to si4n. The Clerk said the Corperation cneld take procending,s in the High Court to compel the magistrates to make the orders. , A Gager strike, or lock-out—for the The Coal "crisis" is not brought about hi Crisis. any aggressive action on the parS -i- -of the workmen—may now, unfortunately, he re-'2, garded as inevitable in the coal trade. The dele',, gates of the three or four hundred thousand ' miners who labour in the districts over which the Miners' Federation holds sway, met in Birming. ham, on Wednesday, and decided to oppose ani reduction of wages. This, indeed, was a foregone' .•.•t conclusion. The miners of the Federation been previously balloted injill their districts, ! had—with the exception of the "raw recruits" Durham and Northumberland--voted with an most absolute unanimitY against compliance vvitV - the demands of the mine-owners. On that therefore, the duty of the delegates was elee1::: ..,..' enough.; they had only to formally register the decision of those who deputed them. It may, deed, be said, that from the moment the mastell,r,o formulated their , demand for a reduction twenty-five per cent. in Wages, a great strike, nr',l. lock-out, was practically certain-'unless a siderable abatement was made upon this vet3l: large order. It was not to be expected that snell terms as these would be tamely accepted bY A large body of workmen, unless it was hopelesell * . disorganised or iiroken by defeat. The Federation is not disorganised nor has it been hopelessly beaten. It is, as nearly every one mits, controlled by able and judicious leaders, an :t''',k 1.1 its members have on more than one occasi°ll 1 •;,. , it given ~ given evidence of disciplined enthusiasm. ' was, therefore, not difficult to foresee that en) demand that has been made could only be e.noi. :`: • , forced by a prolonged and disastrous industil battle. It has been suggested that in giving notice of a twenty-five per cent. reduction coal-owners were really thinking of ten or fiftee: per cent. This, as we know, is the policy of tb, ,'.f.. itinerant pedlar. That übiquitous individual very much in the habit of asking a price for In; commodities which is two or three times high,: •', than be really expects to, receive. If he iinef'f'.. 1 peetedly gets all that he asks, he plumes hien upon his smartness; if not, then he is quite willit 1 to settle differences by the well-understood proee'', of biggling. But, although the peddtiug fraterniq may find many advantages in this method 4P, doing business, it is not a desirable method to 0.11; low in industrial disputes where extensive, and, some respects, national interests are involved. .es• :,..,,,,f. a reduction of ten or fifteen per cent, would the necessities of the employers it would have beet..,'l. better if they had said so at the cornmencenlen.i,,,' Organised as the miners are, a demand for,',:: i twenty-five per cent reduction made a strsl7,.;' inevitable, whereas if the demand had been for. ten or fifteen per cent, the door might have b ~•,e,.. left open for mediation or arbitration. It is, ever, to be said that, so far as can -be judge' ''' Z' oftl,o, r their utterances, many of the larger mine-ows are disposed to insist upon the whole of the rednril:.', tion asked for. /f that be so the, strike is like,' to be one of unexampled extent and bitteree'-',' ..e and one which will 'arrese and disorganise indnstrf:`,7 . over a large part of England and Wales. ..

BOY SCALDED AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday, HPary Lacey, aged 15 years, son of George Lacey, of 26, Bridge-st., Runcorn, was engaged in opening a window in the wash-house, when his toot slipped into the boiler containing hot water, and he was badly scalded up to the knee. DEATH OF MISS COOK, OF HALTON. At midnight on Tuesday, Miss Cooper aged 65 years, succumbed to a long illness. For nearly quarter of a century the deceased occupied the position of use- keeper at Norton Priory, and for some years had lived, at Halton, retired from active services. ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WIDN-ES. • Yesterday, at the Widnes Police Court, Peter Kelly, a violent character, was remanded on a charge of unlaw- fully wounding his wife Bridget, on VS, ednesday after- noon. The woman was unable' to appear. It was stated that her body was one mass of bruises caused by her husband's brutality.

A RUNCORN POACHER. At the Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, before Messrs. J. l3rundrit and H. Reynolds, Thomas Ly diate was charged under a warrant for non-appearance to a summons, on the sth September, 1892, for being found in Unlawful possession of a rabbit and a ferret, at Halton, on the 28th August. Tne case was proved by P.C. Fryer. Fined ss. and 14s. 8 L costs, or 14 days' hard labour.

BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. The annual treat given to the scholars of the above institution took place on Wednesday, when 400 children travelled by special train to Frodsharn. They proceeded to Overton Hill, where si•veral hours were spent in a variety of games. During the afternoon they partook of tea, kindly provided by the senior superintendent, Mr._ 40110 Simpson. A thoroughly enjoyable afternoon was spent.

div.head: ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL WORKS.
div.p: ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL WORKS.

About nine o'clock on Wednesday morning, an acci- dent which might have attended with serious results happened on the Big Field Section of the Manchester Ship Canal works. A number of waggons laden with a variety of materials, drawn by the engine Trafford,were passing the pumping shed when the contents of one of the trucks came into contact with the wooden strueture.

tearing a portion of itaway, and ausing several wag- gons to be. overturned and thrown off the line. The road was blocked for sometime. Fortunately, the men en- gaged in the engine shed escaped unhurt.

div.head: _FALL INTO A QUARRY AT RUNCORN:
div.p: _FALL INTO A QUARRY AT RUNCORN:

_ An accident happened to Mr. thinning' aged 65 years, of Bold-st., about nn on Wednesday. Ile was coming from the farm connected with +Grange Big Pool, Run- corn, by way of the Bridgewater Quarry, which has not been used for some time, when lie, fell a distance of twelve feet, and was found later on in an unconscious [Condition by Mr. Sweetman, who conveyed him to his home. Dr. Robinson found his patient suffering from severe shock to the system. No bones were broken. Be now seems little the worse for the mishap. 1 Sr. MICEILEL'S CIII7IICIL. DITTON. A beautiful new baptismal font has been placed in -St. Michael's Roman Catholic Church, Ditt.m, this week, by Messrs. J. and IV. Hartley, architectural and ecclesias- tical sculptors, St. Helens. The font is circular in fprin, and consists ot a richly-menilded base of Sicilian marble, which carries a red granite polished shaft, the cap of which is of white alabaster with carved foliage of very chaste design. The cap supponting the howl is also of polished Sicilian marble with a bold mould. The font has a beautifully figured oak cover, with polished braes scroll terminal.

Sr. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN BRANCH '1 The lectures in connection with the " Nursing CleiSA.' which have been recently delivered by Dr. McDougall, have been brought to a conclusion. The class has been exceedingly well attended, there having been an average attendance of 40 ladies, who have shown great interest and intelligence as the lectures have progressed. The examination should have been conducted on Monday, but it was deemed advisable to postpone the event for a few weeks, in order to give those desirous of enter- ing for examination time for preparation. Dr. °ken, of Winsford, has been appointed examiner.

div.head: TRICKING A WIDNES POSTAL OFFICIAL.
div.p: TRICKING A WIDNES POSTAL OFFICIAL.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Letitia Fox, a young married woman, of Victoria-st.,was charged with stealing 103. by means of a trick, from Miss Gillow, counter clerk at Widnes Post Office. On Saturday night the prisoner entered the Post Office and requested the clerk to give her a sovereign for twenty shillings in silver. This was done, when the prisoner slipped a half sover.eign on the counter, and said, "See what you have given me ?" Miss Gillow replied that she had given her a sovereign, but the woman persisted so strongly in her statement, that she at last accepted the half sovereign and gave the prisoner another sovereign. Subsequently, when balancing her cash, Miss Gillow discovered that she was 103. shcrt, and information was given to the police. Tile prisoner admitted the offence, and she was fined £1 or 14 dasB' hard labour.

VIOLENT ASSAULTS ON WIDNES POLICEMEN.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, a young man named Richard Tonkies of Wright-street, was cnarged with assaulting P.C.'s Cranshaw and Martin. On Mon- day night P.C. Crenshaw met the prisoner in Church- street and attempted to take him into custody on a commitment which was out against him. The prisoner struck him in the stomach with his wooden leg, knocked him to the ground ; bit him on the hand and otherwise brutally assaulted him. Owing to the conduct of the crowd, the prisoner got away. Early next morning P.C. Martin. in company with P.S. Strickland and P.C. Cranshaw went to the prisoner's !muse and arrested him. On the way to the police station he assaulted Martin by biting him severely. There were 22 previous convic- tions against the prisoner, several for violent assaults and he was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour on each charge.

div.head: FRER MASONRY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FRER MASONRY AT RUNCORN.

The members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons (758) celebrated the festival of St. John on Thursday evening at the Masonic Hall, Devon- shire Square. Bro. John Smith Burgess was installed as w.M., the ceremony being impressively carried out by Bro. Phillips and Bro. Annett. file Worshipful Master then invested the following officers: Bros. C. Phillips, I.P.M. ; W. Hankinson, SW.; a. Linaker, J.W. ; W. R. Wass, P.M. re-elected treasurer; T. H. Annett, P.P.G., Treas., re-elected secretary; A. Salkeld, S.D. ; W. Upton, J.D. ; R. Clarke, 1.G.; James Littler, P.M., organist; Captain Le Couteur, almoner; T. Lydiate. tyler. 1. Coxhill. P.P.A.D. of C., director of ceremonies ; F. W. Clarke, steward. The brethren subsequently partook of a recherche dinner, and the customary loyal and masonic toasts were pro- posed and appropriately honoured. In the course of the proceedings, Bro. Phillips was presented with a past masters jewel and a life governorship of the Cheshire Masonic Educational Institution, in recognition of his services as W.M. during the vast year. The annual picnic will take place on the 27th inst., when Rhyl will be visited.

If you want your WITCH REPAIRED by skilled werkraea take it ti PRITCHARD'S.—Advt FUNERAL OF MISS MANSELL, OP RUNCORN. Amid many demonstations ot mourning and respect the mortal remains of Miss Hannah Mansell, for 18 years head mistress of Runcorn National Se.hools, were com- mitted to the wave at Runcorn Yarish Church on Wednesday afternoon. The deceased lady who had been in frail health for some months, consequent upon a fractured leg, succumbed to an acute attack of diarrlicea on Sunday afternoon' despite the medical skill of Dr. Barron of Liverpool and Dr. Mangan. while giving every satisfaction to those by whom she was employed, by her efficient work, she earned the respect and esteem of her numerous scholars and of all with whom she was brought in contact. The funeral cortege started from the residence of Mrs. Tonics in Lard-street at four o'clock, and proceeded to the church through an asvenue of 300 scholars. In the procession were managers of the schools, schoolmasters and schoolmistresses from the National and other schools, past and present teachers and scholars, numerous personal friends and a number oFrelations. The impressive service was conducted by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood and the Rev. C. F. Montgomery and at the grave side the scholars sang the hymn "0 God our help in ages past." The coffin was hidden beneath floral offerings in the shape of wreaths, crosses and anchors, forwarded by sympathising friends. _

div.head: PLUGGING A DRAIN AT HINGSLIIY.
div.p: PLUGGING A DRAIN AT HINGSLIIY.

At Runcorn County Curt on Tuesday, before his honourJudge Ffotilkes, George Outram, shoemaker of Kingsley, sued Edward Alderman, coal dealer, Green- bank, Kingsley, for £lO 10s. for damage alleged to have been caused by the defendant stopping up a drain. It appeared that the parties lived next docr to each other and owned their respective dwellings. In January 1892 the defendant sold his cottage to a Frodsham ironmonger named Rothwell, whose tenant he became. On the 12th January, a wan who was acting under the defendant's orders was seen working at a drain, which was put at the rear of the cottages for the purpose of running the water trom a disused well. On the following morning plaintiff's house was flooded to a depth of four inches, and the house remained in this state until the 25th March. The flooding had caused serious damage to the property and the damp had calmed Injury to both the plaintiff's and his wire's health. The defendant's atten- tion was drawn to the stoppage in the drain, but he refused to allow the drain to be examined. Eventually, after the defendant had given up possession of his cot- tage to Rothwell, the drains were opened, and it was discovered that three pipes had been taken up and the plaintiff's end of the drain had been stuffed with five coal sacks and some tiles.—His Honour held the opinion that the defendant had caused the drain to he plugged, and he gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the amount claimed, with costs.

ALLEGED RECKLESS FIRING AT A SHIP CANAL The. . _ _

A few days ego, about 3.45 in the afternoon, the Manchester Ship Canal Company's steam tug Walton was passim. down the Mersey from Warrington. When the steamer was about 150 yards on the Dit- ton side of Runcorn Bridge, near where Widnes and Warrington Volunteers were practising shooting . on their range, and aboat fifty yards from the Lan- cashire shore, a shot struck the boat on the star- board side, passed through the engine house, and out at the port into the river. In ita passage the bullet narrowly missed striking the steam pipe,and the engineer had a most fortunate escape. He was leaning out of the port window at the time, and the shot passed about nine Inches above his head, giv- ing him a severe fright. The affair was reported to those in command of the corps. The sergeant-in- structor was deputed to investigate the matter,and that officer has made an inspection of the tug, and he states that the missile which has penetrated its sides were fired from a Martini-Henry rifle. It has transpired that on the afternoon in question some recruits from Warrington were at practice on the Widnes range, and the assumption at, the time was that there must have been a reckless discharge of a rifle. This opinion was founded on the fact that the direction from whence the bulle came was quite opposite the direction of the target from the tiring point. The Volunteer authorities at Warring- ton deny the charge altogether as far as their own men are concerned. Some Warrington recruits were on the range on the afternoon in question, under the charge of Instructor Barker, who says none of the men with him tired at a passing boat. Tun YACHT BR/MM.—ITS CREW Dnowit ED. The yacht Bessie, which for a long time was owued by Warrington boatmea and moored at Bank Quay, capsized on Saturday last, at Crosby, Liver- pool, aad its three occupants were drowned. It is not known how the accident occurred,. UV.: that it had occurred was ascertained from the discovery of the dead bodies of the crew on the beach on Tues- day. The boat was sold more than a year ago to two men named Collinbridge and Temkins, of Man- chester, neither of whom had had the slightest ex- perience in the management of a boat. For a long time .1. Green, of Bank Quay, who was always kaown as Bessie's captain, sailed the boat for the two new owners. But during the present season the owners procured the services of a friend named Price,, of Market Drayton, to sail the craft, which was still kept at Warrington. The inability ef the three men to manage the boat soon became a theme of conversation amongst the local boatmen, for on several occasions the yachtsmen had been unable to get their.boat beyond Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co's when favoured with tide and wind. Some weeks ago, however,t hey had the boat removed to a moor- ing at Widnes. The latter ,end of last week they sailed from Widnes intending, so it is said, to at- tempt a cruise down the west coast. Apart from the inability of the men to manage the boat, the construction of the craft stamped such a venture as unwise, and almost foolhardy. The boat must have capsized a few hours after putting off--pro- bably in one of the squalls that were blowing at the time. At the inquest which was held upon the bodies on Tuesday, a verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. CARPETS and LTNOVEL-MS rnsde and fitted free of charge during site at J. and W. figcoVERY OF A WATCH: A RESCIILIAR, CABE. At the Warrington o:aunty Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Floulkes, John Kelly, 21, Upper Bank-st., sued James McPhillips, 31, Dol- man's-Idle, for the'specific return of a Boston lever watch.—Mr.A. Browne, who appeared for the plain- tiff, explained that the plaintiff and defendant, in the month of June, 1891, lodged together at 21, Upper Bank-at. with a man ?limed Frainey. In October, 1891, plaintiff had decided to return to Ire- land. He packed up his box, and put his watch inside, but did not lock the box until just before proceeding to the station. He left 'Warrington by the 10.10 p.m. train o Holyhead. On opening the box on his arrival in Ireland, he found that the watch was missing,but allowed the matter to stand over until he returned to England in June, 1892, when he came to lodge at the same addtess. One day he was passing the clefendant's house, when defendant was standing at the door with a watch in his hand. Plaintiff asked to be allowed to see it, when he discovered that it was the watch, which he had lost. Plaintiff asked defendant to give it him, but defendant replied that Frainey had given it to him in exchange for a clock, and he therefore declined to return it. Plaintiff went away soon afterwards to Oldham, and returned to Warrington in September, when he again asked for the watch. Defendant said that he would try to fin 1 Frainey, and try to get the clock back again. Plaintiff again went to Ireland anthreturned in June this year,and again demanded the watch. As he was refused the present action was commenced.—Plaintiff's story was corroborated by Patrick .Mannion,vvho saw the watch pieced into the box, and also about two months afterwards deposed to sseing defendant with the watch, when he exclaimed, " Why, that's Jack Kelly's watch," to which defendant made no reply.-111r. Forshaw, for the defence, said that his instructions were, that the plaintiff on going to Ireland, was accompanied to the station by defen- dant and Frainey. On the platform, plaintiff gave the watch to Frainey, who afterwards exchanged it with defendant for 'a clock.--Defendant corrobo- rated this statement, and his wife was also called. —His Honour, in deciding the case, said that the gift of the watch to Frainey was not clearly proved, and therefore the plaintiff was entitled to its spe- cific return.—The watch was handed over in the court. •

div.head: PRIMROSE PETE AT APPLETON.
div.p: PRIMROSE PETE AT APPLETON.

The annual tine in connection with the Appleton Habitation of the Primrose League took place at Appleton Hall, the residence of Mr. T. 11. Lyon, on Thursday. There was a good number of people pre- sent during the day, and they were favoured with beautiful weather. In the afternoon, various games were indulged in, and the Bluecoat School band played selections of music. Tea was partaken of in the large marque, catered by Mr. Speakman. of ths Saracen's Head, Stockton Heath. The annual meet- ing was afterwards held, Mrs. T. IL Lyon, ruling councillor of the habitation, occupying the chair. The following officers were re-elected : Mr.s T. 11. ,Lyoti, ruling councillor ; Mr. Matson, secretary ; and Mr. Logan Wright, treasurer. The committee ' and various other officials were also re-elected. Mr. Logan Wright then addressed the meeting on political questions, more particularly on the Home ' Rule controversy. He contended that the Home Rule Bill had not the support of the majority of Englishmen, Scotchmen, or even of radical Wales. It was a majority simply of Irishmen. A resolu- tion.of censure upon Mr. Gladstone's government was passed unanimously.—After the usual votes of thanks were passed, the meeting broke up, and dancing wasenjoyed until a late hour, the Bluecoat School band supplying the music.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE WORK AT LATCHFORD.

Rapid progress is being made with the work which Still remains to be done on the Latchford section of the Ship Canal. The swing bridge at this point was turned across the canal on Tuesday morning, about half past seven, and as soon as this can be used for vehicular traffic, the bridges in use at present near to, will be removed. The approaches to the new swing bridge have not yet been made, but the road Which leads to it at each end have been completed. Several workmen are at present busy paving the road for vehicular traffic on the bridge, with wooden blocks, and the stranger is soon made aware of that fact on reaching the bridge, by the smell el tar, which is being boiled at each end of the bridge. The parapets on the bridge which have been cemented, are now finished. It is expected the bridge will be in use in the course of a few we. ks. The rails of the old railway of the L. and N.W. Co., have been pulled up, and the steam navvies at work, have now cut through the old line where it crosses the canal, and will before long have extended to the full width of the canal, but it will be some time before the required depth has been reached. The ground at this point is very rocky, and blasting has been resorted to. The continuation of the highway running along the course. of the canal, which crosses the old railway lines and continues under the railway bridge which spans the canal, is now being proceeded with. The old Latchford railway station, at the present time presents a desolate appearance, theonly occupants of the platform being a few dingy milk-cans. It is proposed to substitute the electric tight for the Wells lights now in use, for working during the night- time.

div.head: • STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: • STOCKTON HEATH.

A considerable number of men are now at work on the Ship Canal at Stockton Heath. The point, where the Old Quay Canal will enter the Ship Canal, just now pre- sents a busy appearance. The foundations for the lock are still being laid with concrete and pieces of rock. The pipes which are to convey water from the Old Quay Canal just under the swing bridge to the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, near Runcorn, owing to that firm insisting on having that water, are now being laid. The pipes will run alanw the course of the Ship Canal from the swing bridge at Stockton Heath to Wal- ton Arches where the water will again enter the 0:d Quay Canal there, and afterwards ti conveyed to Messrs. Steele's works. The awing bridge is now complete, but it is not yet known when it v.ill be used for traffic. An accumulator is being built near the swing bridge, in which will be placed machinery for the manipulation of the Icckgates which are to admit vessels from the Ship Canal to the Old Quay Canal, which proceeds to Howley Quay. Near to Tom Paine'a Bridge a large number of water pipes, belonging to the Warrington Corparation.and which are to tun underneath the canal. are now lying on the road, hut the work of laying them has not yet been cominenced. The electric light, in lieu of the Well's lucigen light, Is being used on the Acton Orange section for working during the night time, but i 3 not required at Stockton Heath, as the work here is only proceeded with during the day time. The new road which is to run along the canal from Stockton Heath to Latchford, is being made, and will before long be completed. The hydraulic pressure h.use which is being built by Messrs. Neill Bros., of Manchester, just beyond Twenty-step Bridge, is now ready for the roof, and a few joiners are at work erecting it.

div.head: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Last Saturday I was at .Llaufairfechan, on a quest that combined a 'modicum of business with 4.nuch pleasure. I had no sooner set foot on. the elation plat- form which is beautifully situated be,tween the ever- lasting hills and the deep deep sea, then 1 reaeived a real hearty Runc3rn greeting, from our townsman Mr. John Weston. It appears that Mr. Weston is just on the point of completing a scheme of sewer- age for the Local Board of blanfairlechan, 'sod a few details may interest, the Runcorn frifmas of the worthy contractor.

. . The scheme provides for the drainage of a very scattered district and no less than five-and-a-half miles of sewerage pipes have been laid, some of them at, a depth of 24 teet. The depth of the trenches however, has averaged from 12 feet to 15 feet. The Making of the trenches has l:4•en beset wit very . great difficult i,es. Tie ground was water- logged throughout, but an even worse impediment !to the progress of the work was the number of boulders that were met with in the pipe line. Some Of these stones weighed many tons, and it was possible in the circumstances nuder which the work had to be carried on to remove them by any other means tban blasting. In a nttmberof instances fourteen shots had to be placed in one stone in order to split it into the necessary fragments.

A novel feature of the scheme is that before the sewage reaches the sea, it has to pass through two tanks. For the greater portion of the district the sewage finds its way into an intercepting tank 450 feet long by 6 feet 4 inches wide, by means of gravitation. In the lower part of the town the ground is very flat, and no fall can be obtained,and this difficulty is overcome by pumping the sewage into another tank 210 ft. long and 4 ft. 2 in.wide by means of gas engines, housed in an admirably con- structed building of Ruabon brick. Thence ' the sewage is ejected into the intercepting tank, from whe,re it is flushed into the sea at periodical inter- vals. In the construction of the tanks and engine house half a million bricks have been used. Several ' engineers of eminence in this profession have in- spected the work, and have described it as one of the most unptecedented pieces of sewerage ever known in the country.

The annual meeting of Runcorn Musical Society, held on Tuesday evening, was of the most harmotff- ous description, as a gathering of such a• society ought to be, but which, unfortunately, they fre- quently are not. It is I suppose an universally ad- mittea fact that while choirs, musical societies, madrigal societies, &c., give pleasure to thousands by their concord of sweet sounds, they are for ever being rent by internecine wets of a more or less serious description. The Runcorn Society, it is pleasing to record, has most successfully passed through one crisis, which appears to have had the effect of binding the members more. closely to- gether, and, as Mr. Bruudrit remarked, It may now be considered one of the permanent institutions of the town. The members had no words but those of praise for the whole of the officers, who were unani- mously re-elected. The President and Mr. Brun- drit, and the conductor, Mr. Crossley, especially came in for ovations. At a private meeting after- wards, Mr. Crossley sketched the outline of a plan for next season's concerts, of a most interesting des- cription. It will ne doubt be made public when more fully matured.

The Widnes magistrates appear in" Truth's 'pil- lory this week as follows :—" Nelson Police Court, Jam ds Burke, charged with committing a breach of the peace by kicking hie wife and causing a crowd to assemble. Ordered to pay costs and bound over. Widnes Police Court. Before Messrs. J, Birchall and H. Gaskell junr. Two men named Hagan und Lea,convicted of sleeping out. Fourteen days each." The contrast between the two cases is certainly very great.

The action taken by the United Alkali Co. in regard to the threatened strike of miners will have a serious effect upon Runcorn and Widnes. The company have issued notices that the whole of their works were liable to be closed on the %th or any subsequent date until after the fuel and salt con- tracts are returned. In Widnes from 7,000 to 8,000 men and boys find employment in the company's .manufactories, and in Runcorn there will probably be a further two thousand. A long stoppage would cause great misery amongst the chainical workers. Far too many lead a hand to mouth existence, and a few weeks of idleness would plunge them into the depths of poverty. It is to be hoped that such extreme measures will be found. unnecessary.

The annual treat to the poor children of Runcorn takes place on Wednesday next, when they will have an outing to Overton Hills. The fund is at present inadequate to the demand and subscriptions will be gladly received at the Town Hall. An appeal for such a purpose should not remain unheeded.

div.head: BREAD WE EAT. GRUESOME REVELATIONS.
div.p: THE BREAD WE EAT. GRUESOME REVELATIONS.

At Marylebone (London) Police Court, on Thursday, evid.eace of a gruesome nature was given during the hearing of a summons against a master baker named Edwin P. Joyce, carrying on business at 58, George-st., Portman Square, who was shmmoned by the Maryle- bone Vestry for using a bakehouse which, on sanitary grounds, was unfit for such a purpose. Jt was stated by ! the sanitary officialsthat, in addition to smellingoffen- sively and being black with dirt. the bakehouse swarmed with blackbeetles and cockroaches, an extraordinarily. large number, and some of them were crawling over the dough in the troughs (sensation). Dr. Wynter Blythe the medical officer of lit alth, confirmed the evinence of • his officers as to the unwholesome condition of the place, which, lie said, showed a general want of cleanliness. The atmosphere was offensive, and he could distinctly recognise the bad smell of blackbeetles (sensation).-- The defendant said that he had been willing to do all that was necessary, and had already obtained two esti- mates.—The tuaglqtrates trade an order for the necrs sary work to be done within six weeks,with two guineas costs.

NEW DEPARTURE IN EXCURSIONS TO THE ISLE OF MAN. —The Railway and Steamboat Companies are to be con- gratulated on the inauguration of a new circular tour, which has• just come into•force. By this arrangement, passengers can now take a circidar tour ticket to Douglas via Fleetwood, or Liverpool, and 'return via Barrow, breaking their journey if they so desire at Ulverston, in order to pay a visit to the tinted English lake district ; or, if they pref,,r it, they can go on the outward journey via Barr..w, and return via Fleetwood or Liverpool, the only reservation hoing, that they shall state at the time of booking, by which route they desire to travel, on the outward and homeward j airney. The journey along the Furness railway is one of the loveliest in the country, and even if tourists have no Dine to spend a few days in lakeland, the journec referred to, will of itself repay the traveller for the few extra pence expended on a cir- cular tour ticket. Particulars Of the arrangements herein referred to, will be found in our advertising columns. The Lord Chief Justice of Ireland, addressing the Grand Jury of Kilkenny county on Monday remarked that. there had been a very tubstantial improvement with regard to serious crime.

A member of the Mertborough School Board apologised on Wednesday night for his non-attendance at a commit- tee meeting on the ground that he bad been assisting his wife to shake carpets. lie. Lord's amendments to the Barbed Wire Fences Bill were on Tuesday agreed to by the House of Com- mons. By this measure barbed wire; which way pro- bably be injurious to persons or animals lawfully using a thoioughfare, will have to be removed.
WARRINGTON AND THE COAL CRISIS.
PROBABLE CLOSING OF WORKS.

As Warrington contains so many forges and wire works, which consume an enormous amount of coal. the impending colliers' strike, if prolonged, will ' without doubt have a very serious effect upon the ' town. In order to ascertain more, positively how • local works would be affected, our reporter paid a , visit yesterday to each of the larger firms .in the I ;own. From his inquiries, it was ascertained that ' Messrs: Monks, flail and Co. will be most seriously affected should the threatened strike become an accomplished fact. The greater part of both the tube works and the forge will certainly be stopped, and probably the whole of the works. This will throw four or five hundred men and boys out of employment. The effect of the strike upon Dallam and Bewssy forges will largely depend upon the supply and prices of the coat when the colliers are "out," but should the strike continue for a month or more, the forgeii will probably he closed. The , same will apply to Whitecross. where they cannot tell positively how mat terS will stand as yet. They have pits of t heir own, which will be closed during the strike. s'ankey Wire Mills and %Quids torks do not require the same amount of coal an the above mentioned firms, as they are engaged principally in the wire manufacture Other smaller firms will be affected in a smaller degree. It is to be hoped. how- ever, that the dispute will very soon be settled, or otherwise the outlook generally for Warrington will be very serious indeed. Tnis is greatly to be regretted as only a few months ago thete was so much distress in the town owing toad trade from which it is only just recovering.

A ROAD RACE & ITS CONSEQUENCES. WARRINGTON CYCLISTS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. On Thursday evening, June Bth, a three mile road race promoted by the Warrington Wheelers club was run, when prizes were competed for. P.C. Millington and Brew of Stockton Heath, decided to catch some of these racers, and summon them for furious riding, and accordingly, these officers waited some distance from the finishing point, and stopped several cyclists, and the sequel followed , yesterday at Lynam Petty Sessions. The little court moth was well tilled with Warrington cyclistel some having come to take their place in the dock, some to give evidence, anU others to watch the case., The three cyclists brought before the magis- trates were George Smith, Mill-lane, Warrington ; Herbert Hayes, Kendrick-st.; and Thomas Forbes. P.C. Brew said at 7 p.m. on .the Bth June, he was near Longshaw's Brow, when he saw the three defendants accompanied by several others, riding at the rate of 17 or 18 miles an hour. lie got hold of Smith's bicycle and had to run about 100 yards with him before he stopped, and afterwards took his name and address. He saw Hayes previously, but did'uotstop him as he knew his name. He 'put his stick out to Forbes, but be did not stop. He afterwards served him with a summons at his work. P. C. Millington corroborated the last witness's statement, and said the cyclists. slowed down when they saw the police. John Herbert Ridgway also deposed to seeing some cyclists riding at 13 or 14 miles an hour, but could , not recognise them. Win. Belliau, Lovely-lane, , Warrington, said he went to see the race of Om Warrington Wheelers, and he accompanied Smith and Forbes along the road, but be was certain they were not riding at more than eight miles an hour, as Forbes had a punctured tyre, which made it im- possible to ride at the speed stated by the police, and had Smith been riding at the speed stated, the officer would not have been able to run 100 yards with him. James Melbourne, James Bullet), Wm. James Doherty, and James Keenan, all Warrington cyclists, gave evidence for the defence, and eon- tended that the defendants had not ridden more than eight miles an houi.. The Chairman (Dr.Brabazon) said they were determined to stop this road racing, but as it was the first offence, the defendants would only be fined 2& fid. each, including costs.

div.head: DR. GUEST GORNALL'S REPORT ON SMALLPDX. •
div.p: DR. GUEST GORNALL'S REPORT ON SMALLPDX. •
OPINIONS OF THE MEDICAL PRESS.

Both the " British Medical Journal " and " The Lancet" of Saturday last have leaders on the report of Dr. Guest Gornall with regard 'to the smallpox epidemic in -Warrington. 'Both journals discuss the relative incidence of smallpox in reference to the causes of its extension, first by personal con- tagion, and second, by air-borne infection. " The Lancet" says :--Dr. Gornall extended his investig- ation to the incidence of smallpox upon an area bounded by an imaginary circle having a radius of 1000 yards from the centre of the hospital, and he further subdivided this area into a series of very narrow zones, by means of circles described every 100 yards from the common centre. On Investigating the number of infected houses in the whole of the borough during the smallpox prevalence, it was found that with- in the special area the proportion of the houses thus in- vaded was 3.6 per cent.of the whole, whilst those attacked outside the area amounted to but 02 per cent, of the whole number. The relative incidence of smallpox within the special area was therefore 18 times greater than on the outside. These facts are extremely instruc- tive, but Dr. Gornall seems to think the facilities for personal infection were in the special case so great that inferences as to other methods of spread should he drawn with extreme caution. Dr. Gornall points out that in the special area around the Hope Hospital there were no peculiarities either of density of poonlation or of commonplace unwholesome conditions which might have rendered it especially vulnerable ; and, indeed, he also shows that exactly similar commonplace unwhole- some conditions must have obtained in other parts of the town. Ile furthermore states that, in his opinion, the non-removal of sufferers to hospital does not account for the number of persons who contracted the disease in the special area. After discussing fully all the consider- ation' involved, he states: " The statistics as to the " relative incidence upon the specially afflicted area and its several parts most clearly agree with what we should expect with air-borne infection as the explanation of our difficulties." In concluding a long articleN " The Lancet" saps: Fortunately, h9,wever, which ever theory be adopted a grave responsibility now rests with any Sanitary Authority which erects a smallpox hospital in a populated area. We commend Dr. Guest Gornall's report to all interested in this subject. "The British Medical Journal" concludes its article as follows :—lt is not possible fram mere perusal of a report to weigh the various facts as they presented themselves to Dr. Gornall in favour of the theory of air- borne infection as against that of direct contact. Per- haps both agencies have been at work, but the report must take its place as a contribution to the literature of the subject and so adding to the data on which the I decision of an important question will ultimately be I based.

CONFIRMATION AT SANK F.Y.—On Thursday afternoon, Bishop Ryle, of Liverpool, conducted a confirmation ser- vice at St. Marv' s Church, Sankey. The service com- menced at 2.45 p.m., when 35 candidates presented themselves. The Rev. E. S. Jackson, Vicar, and Res. J. R. Jones,were in attendance. The church was crowded with an interesting throng of spectators. Tim VICTORIA Dissma.—Collections were made on Sunday at Bt. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, in aid of the families Of the seamen who lost their lives in the Victoria disaster. The collections were taken morning and evening. Two very tine sermons were rreached by tie Eov. E. S. Jackson and the collections reached a very satisfactory figure. TANNING CO.'S Trtne,—On Saturday last the onploves of the Penketh Tanning Co. had their annual trip. The piano chogen this year was Blackpool, and at an early hour the men and their wivea and families assembled at Fiddler's Ferry station and proceeded in the special train which had been chartered. The journey •'as rather tedious owing to a long delay at Preston, the party finally arriving at their destination about 10 a.m. The various places of amusement were visited, and many of the trippers enjoyed a " dip" in the sea. The parry started home about 7 p.m., and arrived a little after 10 o'clock. The " outing "was thoroughly enjoyed by all, the fine weather adding not a little to the pleasures of the day. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN-
AT WARRINGTON.

It will be of interest to know that Mr. ,John ' Bennett, son ef Mr. Bennett of Bewsey, has been appointed connexioual evan&list by the Wesleyan conference now being held at Cardiff. I Mr. John Bennett, or the Rev. Mtn Bennett, as he now is, is very popular among the Warrington and the district, as a preacher, and his friends will be delighted that he has been appointed to such an honeurable position, as there are drily four connezional evangelists, viz : Revs. T. Cooke, T. Waugh, Davidson and J. Bennett appointed by conference. air Bennett made his first public appearance on the platform as chairman of one of the missionary meetings at 80ld-street some years ago. lie was at that time at a situation near Leeds. He made a very good impression by his speech or that occasion, and subsequently he occupied the pulpit at several chapels in the Warrington circuit, with such marked success, that the ministry was evidently the right place for him. tie • came to Warrington and for two years he was on the circuit plan as a local preacher, preparatory to entering college.

Lu 160, he finally passed the examination neces- sary to enter the college at Didsbury, where he has been during" the three years required by the Can- ference. During his probation at the college, lie has conducted numerous mission and revival ser- vices,and his success in that work has been so great, that he was evidently the right man for a Conae- xional evangelist, whose work it is to go about the United Kingdom organising revival services. This was the work also that he had set his mind • upon, and it will, therefore, be gratifying to his numerous friends that he should have obtained his , heart's desire, immediately on leaving college. His life now will be .a very wandering one, as he will nbt remain more than a month at most, in one place at once. The work, however, is one in which he takes great delight,ancl he will doubtless make a most successful evangelist. He is a very vigorous preacher, .and ig also very fluent.

Mr. J. Champness who gave his popular lecture on "Some leaves from the diary of an Evangelist' is a brother of the Rev. Thomas Cheapness, the ' founder and organiser of the Joyful News Evange- listic Mission, which has evangelists all over Eng- land and some in South Africa, India and China. Mr. J. Champnese is not very well known in War- ' rington, although at Cadishead, only seven miles away, he resided for some years, and was one of the leaders in religious circles in that village. That is a long time ago, however, but he is still remembered for the earnestness with which he went about his work. After a long period of evangelistic work, he has settled down in Southport, and this year he has been elected as one of the members of the represen- tative session of the Wesleyan Conference at Cardiff.

--- Some time ago,a correspondent in the `.Evaniiner" alluded to the formation of a Brotherhood of Poets• and also indulged in a half concealed hint that Warrington would probably soon ploduce another poet laureate. Well. I don't know much about these strange beings called versifiers, but recently two or three of them have produced some pretty verses. In a publication printed by the Brother- hood of Poets, there are two or three single verses by Mr. R. Storey of Warrington. I quote the fol- lowing, called "Sweet Thoughts."
" Sweet thoughts are the respirations of God Perfuming the garden of man's heart ; Wafted from the Eden of eternal bliss, And designed to itnparadise all worlds."

There are several local members of this Brother- hood of Poets, but they are evidently "respectable poets," and not the kind of which there is at pre— sent a large summer crop, who steal into the editor unawares, with their ragged apparel, their dilating eyes, and wild ambrosial locks, accompanied by reams of their rhythmed inflation.

A very commendable scheme for raising funds in support of the Infirmary and Dispensary has been promulgated by the Workingmen's Committee. It is the organization of what is intended to be a brass baud contest, open, I believe, to all bands. This year the competition will be held on the Recre- ation Ground in Bank Park, on the 26th August. Several well known bands have entered the lists, I believe, and if a few more donations are sent to Mr. Taylor, the secretary—why, the prizes will be all the more valuable, and the success ot the affair will be all the more enhanced. lam sure the Com- mittee merit public support in this matter.

A great hub-bub was made during the early part of the week in consequence of a bullet shooting right through a Ship Canal tug boat, when near Runcorn Bridge. The bullet entered the starboard side of the craft, passed just over the engineer's head and made an exit through the port aide of the vessel. It appears that at that time there was it number of " raw recruits" undergoing firing prac- tice on the shooting range on Ditton Marsh, and the authorities—or some part of them—jumped to the conclusion that the ahot had come from the rifle of one of the recruits. Upon inquiring intothe affair, facts were brought to light which prevented the accident being fastened on to the recruits, but for all that they do not appear to have been publicly exonerated from blame. This should be done, especially in face of the facts which amoant to this, that it was impos,ihle for the shot to come from a Warrington recruit. In the first place, the po4ition at. which the man were firing was such that the boat was practic:ally behind them. Serg- eant-Insl motor Barker testifies that i.o sho: was fired accidentally in the direction of the boat, for there was no rifle discharged except under his immediate supervision. The only remaining alternative was that the ball had rebounded from some hard sub- stance it struck. But this is quite impossible, for the ball would have either rebounded into the air, or been so spent in force as to simply roll from the substance struck. I hope the authorities hare not lost sight of the fact that there is a considerable amount of bird shooting done on that part of the river, and that, maybe, the person responsible for the shot could be found in another direction.

I have been asked by a person who " has hie 1 doutts about vaccination," what I think of a base, or rather, a number of cases reported from Black- burn. At that town several parents were prose- cuted for neglecting to have their children vaccirf- ated, and the person who appeared on behalf of the defendants is said to have produced certificates of the deaths of a Il'lMber of children who had died from smallpox after having been successfully vac- cinated. It was also stated that in all these oases the deaths were reported in the official figures as those of children who had died un-vaccinated. In one case the certificate gave the date of successftil vaccination two days before the child was actually born. Well !to tell the truth I have not thcmglit much about it. On the face ot it, it seems as though the official figures with regard to vaccination were —in Blackburn at all events—got up very carelessly to say the least of it. But, then, what is the official explanation ? There are two sides to every ques- tion.

div.head: TERRIBLE SCENE. SWEPTAWAY BY A RISING TIDE.
div.p: A TERRIBLE SCENE. SWEPTAWAY BY A RISING TIDE.

—• It was a terrible scene which was witnessed at Great Crosby on Monday aftern )ou when the discovery was made that three young 'a Is, pup.ls of Merchant Tailor's School, who had gone down to bathe, had found theea- selves in a position of great peril. They had landed on a mudhank only 150 yards from the water's edge ; but the wind was blowing strong, and the tide was rolling in with terrific force. A great crowd speedily gathered on the beach, but they were powerleas to help. Meanwhile the cries of the poor boys for help could be heard, while the wind was increasing in power,"and the water was steadily rising around them. At last the men of the neighbouring Coastguard station were able to get out a punt, but it was found impossible to mike way in such a craft against wide and tide. They contriyed,however. to reach a boat which was lying at moorings, and & shout of joy went forth from the spectators when it was perceived that see was beginning to make way with the Coastguard men aboard. Onward, onward, they pulled straining eery ner,e, but unhappily when the rescuers were only sixty or eighty yards from the bank, a wave swept the poor lads off their feet, and carried them away before their eyes. An unsuccessful attempt was made to seize them tie they drifted Past. Two men then plunged info the sea, and succeeded in resciulFo°3 , boy, but the other two—Arthur Winslow, age and 'Norman Kruger. aged 13—disappear5d• Their bodies have since been washed •aslmre. The boy saved was a oudger brothel' of Kruger..

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
PROMISCUOI79 BORROWING.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, before Mr. John Burgess (in the chair), and Alderman Chandley, George Webb, a bricksetter 1 Priestley-st., was charged with stealing from A building in Longford- et., on Wednesday the 12th inst., a pointing trowel value 6d. and a brick hammer value is. the property of Enoch Morgan, and also with stealing on Thursday, a lump hammer, value 2s. 6d. the property of John Cooper. From the evidence of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) it appeared that the complainants worked at the same job in Longford-st. On Thursday, Cooper who resides a Stockton Heath, missed his hammer, and at the same time Enoch Morgan missed his hammer and painting trowel. Information was given to the police and P.C. Turner made inquiries and found that Webb had pledged the articles at Mr. Morton's pawnshop, where prisoner bad been in the habit . of pledging his own tools, and when questioned by the shop assistant he said they were his own.. P.C. Turner received the articles and went to the buildings in Longford-st., and arrested the pris- oner. In reply to the charge of stealing the articles he replied" I only borrowed them." Nothing was known of the prisoner before except that he was rather addicted to drink. The magistrates fined prisoner ss. and costs in each case which amounted to £2 103. or 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: BARBERiI VOW..
div.p: A BARBERiI VOW..

Torn Barter, w 11-kno am to the p.ree, was charged at the Oecasio tsl C tut on Monday, with having on apt 7th November, 1892, threatened to shoot Constable Mil- lington while acting in the execution of his duty.—The officer said the prisoner was apprehended as he left Walton gaol that morning, where he had been imprisoned for another offence. On the day in question, witness was at Grappenhall when he saw prisoner and another man in search of game in the daytime. He went up to the, men, when the prisoner, pointing a gun at him, said he would blew his head off if he advanced another yard. The prisoner then went away, but was followed by the officer. Iriarber, however, made his escape. A warrant was at once taken out for his apprehension. The prisoner, who denied the offence, was remanded tol Daresbury Petty Sessions for trial.

div.p: TRYING TO GET A GOOD DINNEI2.

George Meachin, 36, Howard-st. and Wm. Jones, 4, Stamford-st.. were evidently on th'e look out for a good dinner at 12.30 on Sunday morning. P.C. Hollings- worth was on duty at that time in Lovelc-lane near Clapgate Farm, tenanted by Mr. Bennett, When on the Bank Quay side of the railway bridge, he noticed some one croEs the road and go along the oath which goes by the railway to the back of the Workhouse. The officer followed, and saw the two men who, to get away more quickly,lef t a bag behind them which contained cabbages and potatoes. Hollingsworth caught Jones, and took him to the house of John Bandies, and then went after Meachin, and brought him to the same house. Jones had meanwhile escaped. Meachin as then brought to the Police Station, and Jones afterwards surrenderod himself. They were brought before the Warrington magistrates on Monday morning, when the Chief Con- stable said in their favour that they were very quiet when captured, although that part of Lovely-lane was so lonely.—Mr. Bennett, who appeared at the court, wished that an example should be made IV the two pri- soners, as he v. as continually having 1118 crops damaged by persons coming during the night. He thought that farmers had enough to contend with in the elements, without .having trespassers as well.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of 10s. and costs, or 14 days upon each prisoner.

div.head: SEIZURE OF BAD FIRE.
div.p: SEIZURE OF BAD FIRE.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Patrick Rearden, fishmonger, was charged with having for sale 315 fluke weighing 1151b5., alleged to be unfit for human food, on July 12. The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) prosecuted, and Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, defended.—The Town clerk said that defendant had a stall in the market. On Wednesday, Inspector Norman was examining the fish stalls, and on coming to the stall kept by defendant ha observed a box of fish un- der the stall. Be examined the box, and found it con- tained 315 flukes weighing 115Ibs. They were quite unfit for human food. Defendant's wife said that she did not intend to sell the fish. Inspector Norman at once seized it.—lnspector Norman corroborated the Town Clerk's statement, and said that the fish was des- troyed the next day.—Examined by Mr. Riley, he said that the fish was not exposed for sale. The fish might have been all right the day before..—Mr. Riley did not deny that the fish was bad, but said that it was placed ready for the cart to be taken away. He thought there should be some common receptacle for the stall-holdersl to nut the bad fish in.—lnspector Norman said that each stall-holder had casks in which to throw fish remnants and bad fish, and carts came each day to take them away. —The magistrates dismissed the case, and wished to call the attention of the Markets Committee to the desirability of having some common receptacle for the fish which was unfit for sale. They thought Mr. Riley had very properly called attention to the need of this.— The Town Clerk said that he would bring the matter before the Markets Committee. COAL LIBELS MISSING. _

George Hankey-,- coal dealer, was charged at the Is ar- rington County Sessions on Wednesday, with having a quantity of coal in bags upon a lurry,in Orford,witbout having tin labels upon the bags, on the 11th inst.,in con- travention of a bye-law of the Lancashire County Coun- cil. Defendant said that his bags had got wet, and hd had to get fresh ones, and therefore had no time to put the labels upon them. He was fined N. Gd. and costs.

Ditircx AND DISORDERLY.—John Jones. Harley-st., Liverpool, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st. P.C. Evans said that defendant was fighting with another man. He was fined ss. and costs. Michael Crane, Crossley-sit., was fined a shnilai penalty for being drunk and disorderly in Crossley-et. P.C. Wood said the defendant was in the street assaulting his wife, and had no shirt on. THEFT OF WATER BOTTLE STOPPERS.—John William Mault, a militiaman was charged with stealing from the Barrack room, on the 17th inst., two water bottle stop- pers, value 3d. the property of the military authorities. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. Sergeant Bullard said a man in his company reported that his water bottle stop- per had been taken. They were metal stoppers, and fixed on the top of wooden bottles, they were valued at lid. each. The prisoner had offered for sale two stop- pers, which he sold for a penny each. Prisoner in reply said he found one of them and the other belonged to his bottle. He was sent to gaol for seven days hard labour. Tnuesome.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman) and Councillor James Fairelough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLIC.—For committing this offence on the previous day, John Higgins was fined 10s. and coats or 14 days ; and George Finney and Annie Quin, ss. and costs or seven days' hard labour. SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.—John Hardman was charged with being a suspicious character, and with being found in the enclosed premises of the Rev. B. B. Prescott, Wash-lane Latchford on the previous evening.—P.C. Corbett said that be saw prisoner look every way to see ' it anyone was about, and then climb over the wall of the Rev. 8.8. Prescott. He examined the back premises of the house and then went into the garden and took an apple. He then returned into the back premises of the house, when he saw P.C. Lewis. He then ran off, and witness and P.C. Lewis gave chase, and prisoner was caught as he was getting over the wall of Mr. Broad- bent's park.—Prisoner was sent to' gaol for twenty-one days. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder- man Wright, Councillors El. Roberts and J. H. Fleming, and Dr. Gernall. • ABSENT FROM TRATNINO.—John Dawson was fined 40s. and costs, or 14 days, for absenting himself from the annual training of the Third South Lancashire on June 23rd, last year. SMACKINO A LITTLE GIRL'S FACE.—Harry and Sarah Broadhurst, 18, Gaskell-st., was summoned by Zebudah Brewer Clegg, a little girl of ten years of age. The little girl with the peculiar name said that the defendants smacked her in the face, and thumped her in the back on the above date. The defendants said that the girl had hit one of their children, and they were simply stopping her. The defendants were each fined in the costs. QUARREL BETWEEN NEIGHEOURS.—Virginia Howell .44, Lythgoe's-lane, was summoned for assaulting and beat- ing Amy Syers, 38, Lythgoe's-lane, on the 12th inst. There was also a cross-summons against Amy Syers. The evidence of the complainant showed that Mrs. Howell had struck her on the head with the brush,owing to a dispute about the children. Mrs. Howell, on the other hand, said that Amy Byers bad struck her. A number of witnesses, who gave very contradictory evi- dence, were called on both sides.—Aiderman flarrison,in giving the decision of the Bench, said that they were of opinion that a great number of lies had been told by one ' side, and they were inclined to think it was on Mrs. Howell's side. They would,therefore,bind over Virginia Howell to keep the peace for six months, and they would dismiss the summons against Amy Syers.
