div.head: CRISIS IN THE COAL TRADE.
div.p: CRISIS IN THE COAL TRADE.

RESULT OF THE BALLOT. The result of the ballot which has been taken by the Miners' Federation on the employers' proposal to reduce wages 25 per cent. shows an overwhelming majority in most districts in favour of a national strike rather than submit to a reduction. The miners in Durham and Northumberland have decided not to acquiesce in a strike, and in the event-et one being declared they will decline to pay any levy whiell the federation may order. , In South Wales .the sliding scale prevails, the federa- tion having so far failed in the efforts it has made, ex• cept in a few instances, to induce the miners to join its ranks, and it is understand that the Welsh miners will therefore remain at work, This will , also be the case with the Scotch miners, who, however, bare decided to , ask for an advance in wages, and to hold a meeting at the close of the month to consider what should be done I in the event of the advance not being conceded. In I the meantime, the men will give in their notices, so that they can cease work if the conference should so decide. In anticipation of a strike being declared by the Miners' Federation ,there has been considerable buying of coal on the part of merchants and others, an prices have gone up materially. This is notably the case in London where quotations for coal have shown a steady risk on, the exchange for more than a week past. ST. HELENS AND THE STRIKE.

About 3,000 employees of the United Alkali Company at St. rielens have received notice that, in consequence of the coal trade dispute, the company cannot under- take to find employfrenb, for them utter the 24th inst. The works niav close 011 that day untilafter the coal end salt contracts are resumed, or if not closed then, they are liable to be closed on any subsequent day without further notice.

On inquiry on Tuesday, the London and Manchester Plate Glass Company stated that the threatened strike may have the effect of stopping some if not all, of the casting halls at their extensive works at Sutton and Ravenhead, St. Helens.

A strong feeling exists in St. Helens that other works in addition to the United Alkali Company will be effected if the threatened strike of the colliers take place. lc is stated that at Messrs. Cannington Shaw, and Co.'s Bottle Works, where about 1,500 hands are employed, conditional notices will be posted stating that the firm will only guarantee work from day to day after a cer- tain date.

The result of the ballot among the St. Helens colliers was mada kn.wn on Tuesday night by Mr. Glover, the miners' agent, as follows : In favour of Against Name of Mine. resistance, resistance. rilkington's (Bolton) Raveushead 404 Plicenix 144 Win teen:it's Astiton's Green 386 Collin's Green Z3B Bold _ _- 2,418 46

There were eight spoilel votes. It will thus be seen that the total ballot was 2,460 out of a probable num- ber ot employees in the St. Helens district,of 2,600. Mr. Glover explains in regard to the twenty-eight votes as *accepting the reduction at Ashtotis 'Green that six weeks ago they had occasion to take a ballot there on a smaller dispute, and the men were asked to record their votes" for a strike or against a strike.' The men, in filling up their papers last week admit they thought they were voting for a strike. •

div.head: RICHARD EVANS AND CO.-NO INTERIM DIVIDEND.
div.p: RICHARD EVANS AND CO.-NO INTERIM DIVIDEND.

Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of Elaydock, Ashton, GolOorne, and St. Helens. issued the following circular to shareholders on Saturday —" Your directors have very carefully considered the question of declaring an interim dividend, and looking to the very serious depression in the coal trade, and having reaard to the impending application of the coalowners for an abso- lutely necessary reduction in wages, they do not con- sider themselves justified in declaring an interim dividend this year.—l am, yours faithfully,-T. GRIUKE.DIUTTON, Chairman of Directors." NORTHUMBERLAND AND•DURHAM.

The Northumberland miners have decided by three to one against coming out oustrike. The result of the ballot of the. Durham miners was made known on Tuesday, as follows :-104 voted in favour of a strike, 386 against, 20 neutral, 125 in favour of paying a levy to support a strike, 212 against, 123 neutral, 291 in favour of conciliation or arbitration, 92 against, 54 neutral. A large majority voted in favour of entirely withdrawina. from the federation.

div.head: CONFERENCE OF DELEGATES.
div.p: CONFERENCE OF DELEGATES.

The Conference of delegates; from the Miners' National Federation on questions connected with the present crisis in the coal trade was begun on Wednesday at Bir- mingham. Mr. B. Pickard, 111. P., presided over 60 delegates, representing 268,400 miners*, out of a total number of miners employed in the different district's from which delegates attended of 460,677. It was stated that the miners in Yorkihire and Lancashire, Derby- shire, Notts, Leicester, and North Wales were under notice, that they were opposed to any reduction of Wages, and were prepared to carry out any resolution that the Conference might come to. The miners in Northumberland, Durham, Cleveland district, Cumber- land, and about 36,000 elsewhere are not under notice. The total number of miners connected with the Federa- tion who have received notice is 218,328. Mr. Aspin- wall (Lancashire) moved a resolution declining to accept any wages reduction. Mr. J. Wilson, M.P. (Durham), proposed as an amendment that the dispute should be settled by arbitration. The resolution was carried by the votes et delegates representing 198,000 miners, as against those representing 50,000. The Northumberland delegates did not vote. A further resolution, that the miners in those districts of the Federation that have suffered reductions in wages should give notice for an advance sufficient to cover the amount of sucn reduc- tions over a period of two years. and failing such notice bhould cease to be mernhers of the Federation, wo also carried by the votes of 199,000, as against those of 50,000. Northumberland again remained neutral. It was further stated that the miners in Durham and Northumberland have not yet been balloted on the ques- tion, but it a strike should ensue a ballat will be taken for or against joining in the struggle.

IMPORTANT NOTICES. The Salt Union, Limited, and Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Company, chemical manufacturers, N3rthwich, have issued notices to the effeet that in consequence of of the threatened strike of the coal miners, the em- ployees must consider themselves engaged as from day to day only. This notice affects about 5,000 men. TIIE BIRMINGHAM CONFERENCE.—THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The miners' conference reassembled at Birmingham on Thursday morning, Mr. Pickard, Ml'., presiding. Mr. Parkinson moved that all work people be advised to re- fuse to fill up any coal that is now in stock during the strike, if such there be. Mt. Frith (Yorkshire) seconded , the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. ' Greenall (Lancashire) next moved that the men in the federated districts who have not received notice of a re- duction tender their notices on the next making up day , to terminate contracts.--This resolution was seconded by J. Murray (Yorkshire), supported by Haslam (Derby- shire), and opposed by Edwards (Midlands). It was carried by 149,000 against 101,000. Delegates were ap- pointed along with the executive to meet the coalowners in London. Mr. Stanley stated that more than 15 per cent, of the Midland• Federation were out of work at pre- sent resisting a reduction in their wages. He applied for these men to be supported by the federation accord- ing to rule. It was thereupon resolved that those men be supported if it is found the require.: number are on strike, but on the motion of Mr. Harvey, seconded by Mr. O'Connor, it was resolved that the coal porters of the United Kingdom be called upon when necessary to refuse to unload coals coming from districts not carry- ing out tlie resolution of the conference. It was also decided that should a strike occur that the men required to attend ponies and wind water should be allowed to work at the old rate of wages, but in no cases to wind coal. The conference concluthid with the usual votes of thanks.

• THE YORKSHIFE COLLIERIES. On Thursday evening, after the Birmingham Confer- ence had passed the resolution to enforce the twentieth rule of the Federation, Mr. Pickard, M.P., telegraphed to the headquarters f the Yorkshire Miners' Association at Itarnsely isstructions to all the miners not under notices at next making up day to tender their nnties. Thirty- two collieries in South and West Yorkshire were also wired to, to tender their mutices. All the Yorkshire collieries are therefore likely to be closed. Close upon 12,000 colliery workers are employed at pits at which no notice has been given, and the situation is be- coming serious. EFFECT ON THE IRON TRADE. On Thursday iron prices in Staffordshire were greatly stronger owing to the Miners' Conference resolutions at Birmingham. The decision that districts which have n't received notice are to give n,tice to leave the pits has taken honmasters completely by surprise, and the outlook has become, increasingly serious. Sheets on Thursday showed advances of from 2s. ed. to 55., and in the event of a strike all manufactured iron prices would quickly run up 5. or 10,4. per ton. , Ironmasters on Thursday refustd to book forward orders, and japan- ners' trunk sheets were declared a I.os.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMEN L.
MONDAY.

lathe House of Commons on Monday, the House went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, taking up con- sideration of clause 27,which prevents the Irish Legisla- ture from interfering with the existing rights of Judges of the Supreme Court, County Court Judges, the Land Commissioners, and other permanent civil servants of the Crown in Ireland. The clause was added to the bill after a number of amendments had been disposed ot. Mr. MonLsr subsequently stated the scheme of the scheme of the Government for dealing with the members of the Irish Civil Service generally. The Labour Disputes (Arbitration) Bill and the Tram- Wave Bill were to have been advanced a stage before the House adjourned, bit they were opposed from the Conservative aide of the House and had to be post- poned.

In the House of Lords the-Earl of ROSEEEERY made a ststemont about the position of Siamese affairs. Ile said that the French Government declared themselves to be not less anxious than ourselves to maintain the independence and integrity of Siam, and that her Majesty's Government would not lose any opportunity of taciiitating a satisfactory solution of the difficulty. The Marquis of LONDONDERRY drew attention to the ad- ministration of justice in Ireland, particularly in county Clare, and contended that the Government ought to re- vive the provisions of the Crimes At which had been revoked. Earl SPENCER said the one aim of the Gov- ernment in Ireland had been to restore law and order, and the condition of the country taken as a whole was much better than it was during the last year the late Government were in office. TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, Mr. Gladstone, questioned as to what steps were being taken to carry out the resolution of the House with regard to the appointment of county magistrates, said it was necessary, for the Lord Chancellor to act in tha matter with care, and he was desirous to work as fares possible in concert with and even through the medium of the Lords Lieutenant, though that was not the limit of hi: action. Already a very conniderable number of magis- trates had been appointed in consequence ol the movemenb associated with the resolution of the House.

The House went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, taking into consideration clause 28, which relates ti the tenure of office of permanent Civil Servants and tin terms of retirement. An amendment, moved by Mr. Balfour, that no Irish official should be dismissed from the service in Ireland until an offer hail been made tt him of a position of analogous kind in the Civil Servict of England or Scotland, was rejectedeby 241 to 199., Mr. Hayden moved an amendment to place half the chargt for pensions and gratuities upon the Imperial Exchequer It was defeated by 251 to 92. Another attempt made by Mr. Mundella after midnight to advance the Trade Disputes Arbitration Bill was frustrated by members ori the Opposition side of the House.

div.head: In the House of Lords the Places of Worship (Sites) Bill was read a third time. WhDNESDAY.
div.p: In the House of Lords the Places of Worship (Sites) Bill was read a third time. WhDNESDAY.

The consideration of the Home Rule Bill was resumed in the House of Commons on Wednesday in Committee. clause 28, making provision for persons holding Civil Service appointments, being further discussed. Several amendments were proposed, but ultimately the Govern- ment carried all their points, and the clause was agreed to, as was also clause 29, .as to existing pensions and superannuation allowances. Mr. MIINDIILLA afterwards moved the second reading of the Labour Disputes (Arbitration) Bill, and that it be referred to the Grand Committee. He appealed to the House, seeing how critical was the condition uf affairs at the present time, to allow the bill to proceed. Sir J. GOMM' objected, and asserted-that the bill was not likely to do much in the way of settling disputes. Mr. MITN DELLA had the support of Sir Albert Rollit and other members, but Sir John Gorst would not give way, the result being the postponement of the resolution.

THURSDAY. • In the House of Commons, on Thursday, Mr. MORLEY in reply to Mr. Bodkin said there was no change in the manner in which Irish criminal statistics were compiled. The practice now followed was that it had obtained for years. Au occasion to criticise the action of the execu- tive, and if opposed to them in politics an English judge would be doubly careful. (Irish cheers.)—Mr. CansoN (amidst cries of 'Notice, notice") asked a number of supplementary questions.—Mr. MORLEY said the House would see that the hon. gentleman must know that he could not answer these questions without notice.—Mr. CARSON: Then you should not attack a judge. (Cries of " Order.") I won't be mobbed by members beloW the gangway. (Loud cries of "Order.') It is a cowardly attack. (" Oh !" and loud cries of "Withdraw.")—The SPEAKER called on the hon. gentleman to withdraw the expression he had just used. (Nationalist cheers.)—Mr. CARSON said that in deference to the directions of the Speaker he would withdraw the observation. Replying to a number of questions Sir E. Grey said there were three French and two British gunboats at Bangkok. An ultimatum has been sent to Siam by France, but her Majesty's Government were not in a position to make any ,announcement as to its terms. I The only part of the eltimatum which concerned Her : Majesty's Government was that which related to terri- torial arrangements. The Government had determined to send Lord Dufferin at once to PariS in order to exo charism viewilin an amicable spirit. Mr. BARTLEY asked a question aleout overcrowding of third-class carriages on the London and North-Wes- tern Railway. Mr. Burt said the company had informed the Board of Trade that there were very exceptional demands on them on the occasion in qaestion. The Board of Trade had no power in theso matters except to call the attention of the company to the fact. Sir E. GREY, replying to questions, said it was under- stood that a ultimatum had been sent by the French Government to the Government of Siam. The only part of the ultimatum which concerned. Her Majesty's Gov- ernment was that relating to territorial arrangements, and they had determined to send Lord Dufferin to Paris to exchange views in an amicable spirit with regard to certain points which seenied to require elucidation. Toe Channel Tunnel (Experimental Works) Bill was withdrawn. The House again went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, and was occupied up to ten o'clock in discuss- ing, clause 30, relating to the constabulary. At that hour the Closure resolution came into operation, and the clause was added to the Bill by 315 to 289. After this two hours and a half was spent in dividing on succeed- ing clauses.

In the House of Lords the Earl of KIMBERLEY, reply- ing to the Earl of Harrowby,said there was no desire on the part of the Government to interfere with or injure Voluntary schools, but they did intend by degrees to bring the schools of the country np to modern sanitary requirements.

div.head: RECENT HULL STRIKES.
div.p: THE RECENT HULL STRIKES.

ACTION AGAINST THE SHIPPING FEDERATION. On Thursday at the Liverpool County Court, before his Honour Judge Collier, the test case of the man John Graham, who was engaged in May last to work at Hull during the dock strikes, against the Shipping Federa- tion was resumed after adjournment frctn last week. The case affected several hundred men. The particulars are that Graham, a,lo'ing with a large body of men, was engaged by the Federation to work a fortnight, and to continue another two weeks if required. At the expir- ation of the first two weeks the men continued to work, but in the middle of the third were suddenly discharged on account of the strike terminating. They were paid up to the time of their dismissal, but claimed the whole month. His Honour held that the contract had been broken by the Federation, and gave judgment for the defendant, with costs on the higher scale. Mr. Taylor, who appeared for the Federation, remarked that he would not advise his clients to fight any of the other cases.

div.head: "BLACKENING A DEAD MAN'S MEMO RN."
div.p: "BLACKENING A DEAD MAN'S MEMO RN."

EXCITING SCENE AT A CONSISTORY COURT. An exciting scene took place in the Chester Consis- tory Court on Thursday on the application by Mr. Brown, solicitor, .Stockport, to insert in St. Matthews, Edgeley. Stockport. a tablet in memory of the former vicar, the late Rev. John Willington. Mr. 'l'. W. Potts opposed on behalf of Thomas Potts and Arthur Henry Sykes, parishioners, on the ground of the conduct and character of the late Mr. Willington. He alleged that the decease was in 1872, as a consequence of misconduct and mode of life, in considerable difficul- ties, and his furniture was sold under distress. He was declared bankrupt, vOth liabilities £1,380, in- cluding £7OO money lent. Mr. Brown protested against this brutal objection and blackening of a dead mates memory, and challenged Mr. Potts to go into the box and prove his slanderous allegations. The widow was in court and Chan- cellor Espin, in adjourning the case, regretted the painful incident.

PRACTICAL SYMPATHY OF AN ANGLO- AMERICAN MILLIONAIRE.

An Anglo-American millionaire, who spends much of his time in this country, and who has recently been in communication with Mr. Saunders, M.P., and other Radical members, as become Er, impressed with the necessity of taxing ground values in London, in order to relieve the taxpayers and free industry, that he has subscribed £5,000 as the nucleus of a fund, which it is hoped will reach £20,000, for the purpose of assisting the candidature of persons able and willing to promote the movement in Parliament, county councils, and ves- tries.

THE NEW PUBLIC 'HALL AT EARLESTOWN.

-- As the imposing looking building erected in Market-Street, and called the "Public Hall," hit t more commonly the 'kTown Hall'" Is rapidly enproacLing completion, and will within the next tew' weeks lenvia the hands 'of Messrs. Neill an,. Sons, Of Stiange ways,' Manchester, a brief decor ip- tion of- the -interior arrangements may perhaps nok be out of place: Approaching it from the lower end ot Market-street, the building bears a very imposing ‘ppearance, the tower with its clock lending a look to someimportance to it. A nearer view, howevet, sons( - what disappoints one, from the fact that the corn, r :looking down Market-street is composed only of windoe s ,trid blank walls, where one would have expected to fit d the main entrance; with a respectable approach to it. The main entrance to the building is from Market-street. : in practically the centre of the structure, whose outside. architecture savours something of the `‘ Queen Anne " style; and yet is a mixture of that end other. periods, but onstlie whole ils appearance is neat and compact. It would be difficult to say what is the shape of the building, but it one were to describe it as something similar to the " Frttemasons " symbols of two squares witlythe corner of one completely takea away they would net be very far wrong.. It is not our wish; how- ever, to find fault, and there cannot be any doubt that the hall and offices when Finished will be an °moment to the town. Mwe have already pointed out the entrance is from Market-street, by a vestibule which is 181 t. by Mt. wide, and approached by three steps, the inside doors being fitted With flibb's patent springs, which enables the doors to swing freely and without any kind of jar: The floor is prettily laid with tiles in a herring bone design with mosaic border, and this brings to the wide and airy corridor from wlecli the offices and other 'codas on the ground gporare gained. Turning to the left bn reaching the corridor we come to the clerk's general office and further on the clerk's private office and office for plans. We next gain the entrance to the . tower. From . the basement to the weather vane the tower stands 100 feet high. We say weather vane, but a stranger unless he has previously I tallied his hearings will have a difficulty in ascertaining from what direction the wind is blowing, as tor some purpose or 'other the prevision of the N.S.E.W. indica- torS have been omitted, but perhaps this will come later on. The tower is of tetra cotta design with copper top and gilded vane, the copper work having been carried out or Messrs. Ewart, of Loudon. It is fitted with a four diel clock, supplied by Messrs. Putt's of Leeds, which will chime the quarter hours. It is supplied with three oetis, the largest of which weighs 12cwt. the two sroaller ones varying in tone, and it is expected it will be in full working order by the first, week in - August, in tact the machinery is now being fixed, audet night each of the dials will be illuminated. Access to the tower is gained from the first floor by four iron lidders, and eaelf of the landing places, are composed of iron girders and concrete. After visiting the tower MI glance at the Surveyor s drawing, and private .ace , the gas testing room, the Committee room, and the Board room, in which there is a moult-tient room for the safe storage of all deeds and other valuable papers le- la,ting to the business of the township. Then we have the nuisance inspector's office, school attendance office. and here we get by a back door into Tamworth-st. But retracing-our steps along the corridor we have varlet s lavatories,Und a waiting room. The dado on the con - dor walls harmonises very neatly with the design of the tiled flooring. The various offices mentioned are of couree bare of any sort of forniture, but the lighting is of an excellent chatacter being composed of Stot, s patent lights. The fire grates have a rich appearatust especially that in the Board room, and with one or two. exceptions have been supplied through Mr. Astley Sir", , of Earlesto n. The flooring is composed of blocks laid in concrete, and the appearance, independent of the wear, is much before the old boarded ,floors. We saw come to the staircase which is composed of the best Aspley tYorkshire) white stone; it is seven feet Wide, and the steps have a tread of 13m. by 7in. and are built into the walls with a bearing of six inches. there are two landings, the hand rail and newels oeing of English Oak, and the balustrades are of iron filigree work. Upstairs we have the large assembly room which is 70 feet long and 35 feet wide, and is ' entered from the first floor by folding spring doors. 'On the left at the end of the Hall, is a spacious platform the full width of the Hall, and approached from the room by two flights of steps. It has a gradual slope to the front. Behind the platform are ladies and gentlemen's retiring rooms, from which access to the platform can be gained. Separate lavatories are also provided, fitted up with every modern convenience. At the opposite end of the Hall, is a capacious gallery, which runs back 1$ feet, the entrance to this being by an iron staircase frotn Tamwortlbst. The assembly room 'slighted by two of Stett's patent lights, with ventilators combined. At the gallery end is a serving room, with lift in connection with the basement, which will no doubt be found most convenient in the event of banquets, dinners and such like. On this floor also there is a retiring room, 34 ft 9 by 18 ft., fitted in the centre with Mallinsons patent sliding doors, so that in a few moments the room can be made available for two separate meetings being held at the same time. The landings and staircase are spi, nrl- - lighted, the top or ceiling, being composel of figured glass. We have now about exhausted the various offices and rooms, and it only remains te say that the drainage of the building is most complete and of the very letest principle of Doulton's patent system with Helleyers traps. The walls 'all through are com- posed of brown glazed and cream bricks, The ventila- tion is also most consplete,being fitted up with Kershaw's patent. All the lavatciries are fitted'. with cold water; but provision has been made whereby a supply of hot watdr can be readily obtained, arid the fittings are cam- , posed of bay-wool We have omitted to-mention that 071 the first floor there is another small retiring room, ' 13ft. square, which can be used for small meetings. The building is heated throughout with hot water, and has been fixed by Messrs. King of Liverpool. In connection with the hall is a porter's, or oiretaker's lodge, which comprises' a kitchen, sitting room, three bedrooms, and pantry, and every modern convenience suitable for such a dwelling. Of course, from the description it will be seen thitt it is the inten- tion of the Commissioners to transfer their headquarters to the tublio Hall,and there is no doubt future results of the general elections will l•st declared from here,as provi- sion line been made by erecting a balcony in front,nearly over the main entrance, from which the defeated and successful candidates can address the crowd. A large yard will be provided and surrounded by a high wall,but this will be built by Mr. Bunting, of Earlestown. It is not yet known when the building will be publicly opened, but it will leave the Contractor's bandit in the course of the next three weeks. It then remains for the Commissioners to furnish it. It would not be amiss Co herald the completion by the ringing of a peal on the

div.head: FAIIILITY IN MARKET STREET.
div.p: FAIIILITY IN MARKET STREET.

A. SCENE WITNESSED BY CROWDS. An inquest was held at the Railway Hotel, Earlestown, on Tuesday, before Mr. S. Brighouse, county . corOner; touching the death of Henry Taylor, aged 1513, living at 62, Wargrave-road, who died on Sunday from the effect of injuries 'received by being knocked down by a waggonette, which was running up Market-st. to the Newton Race. Course on Saturday, July Ist. On that day about half- past one, the deceased was crossing Market-st., near the new Townlfall. At that time the street was thronged with vehicular traffic and, pedestriays. A waggonette driven by a man named Daniel Westhead. of Rambo-- long, Came up and knocked deCeased to the ground. The driver was warned by the shouts of the crowds of people in the street of the danger of the unfortunate man, but, in trying to stop the horse, his feet slipped the foot- ! board and befell forward between ' the horse and the .shafts. Taylor was removed to a house in Tarnworth- st. and attended by Dr. Valentine, but subsequently was under the care of Dr: Patterson. Despite every atten- tion, however, he died. Daniel Westhead, the driver of the waggonette, gave evidence, and stated that lie was going up Market-St. from the station to the Newton races with ten passengers in the conveyance. There was a great deal o: -traffic on the road. On hearing the shouts of the people he attempted to pull the horse up, but his feet slippeclou the footboard and he fell forward. Ue did not know there had been an accident until he yot up. A f ter.a Short dOiberat ion the jury returned a ver- dict of " Accidental.death" and I.xonerated the driver from blame. The Coroner, in reviewing the evidence, said it did not seem to be generally realized by drivers that conveyances had only a secondary right to the road. Ikot passengers had the first claim on it. •

div.head: SAD DEATti OF A_ BOY AT ST.
div.p: SAD DEATti OF A_ BOY AT ST.
HELENS.

-777" BURIED IN A SAND SHOOT. About sdven o'clock on Tuesday night, Win. Doyle Robinson, aged 11 years. son of George Robin ' son a Wh flotman, ose home is at 13, Bradshaw-street, Man cheater, met with a sad death at the Packet Nook Glass- works, St. 'Helens, belonging to the Union Plate Glass Company. During the holidays the little fellow had been with an uncle, named Wm. Gibbons, on the fiat Fanny, which on Tuesday morning arrived at St. Helens • with a load of sand from Eastham„ The sand was lifted from the boat, and then dropped down a shoot, which holds about 50 tons. Robinson was playing on top of the shoot, and although the workmen cautioned him as to the danger, he cmtinued there. About a quarter to seven, his cousin, Joseph Henry Gibhon,a,ged 16, saw him sinking in the sand, which closed round him. Gibbon called for assistance, but the body could not be recovered for half an hour, and life was then extinct.

div.head: – MR. GLADSTONE AND MR. BURNS.
div.p: - MR. GLADSTONE AND MR. BURNS.

The London correspondent of the "Manchester Guar- dian" records that a pleasant interchange of 'courtesies between Mr. Gladstone and Mr. John Burns was wit- nessed In the Government division lobby the other night. While the fifth of a long series of divisions was progress- ing, the Prime Minister was in the crush of members waiting for the doors to open in the narrow portion of the lobby which separates the turnstile from the tellers.' some minutes had to elapse before any forward move- ment was possible, and in this interval Mr. Gladstone entered into conversation with his near neighbour, sat- ing, amongst other things, how satisfactory the first two divisions had been for the Government. Suddenly the personality of the man to whom he was talking seemed to come home to the right hon. gentleman, and turning suddenly, he asked, "Have I the pleasure of speaking to MK Burns?' The answer being in the affirmative, Mr. Gladstone asked', "May I shake your hand?" and then he went on to tell pathetically how his sight was failing, and how at times it was simply by something in the con- tour of the person or in the tone of the Yoicethat he was able to recognise anybody. From this the, conversation passed to other things, until the doors opened, and the mass of Members streamed past the tellers. One thing said by each of the interlocutors is worth preserving. " Hard work," said Mr. Burns, " makes work, and makes one love it," to which sentiment, so much after his own heart, the Grand Old Man replied, "May you live for many, many years, Mr. Burns, to put that prin- ciple.into practice."

div.head: RAILWAY DISASTER NEAR BLACKPOOL. A STRONG VERDICT.
div.p: THE RAILWAY DISASTER NEAR BLACKPOOL. A STRONG VERDICT.

_ The Coroner's inquiry into the circumstances of the railway accident at Poulton on July 1, by which three persons were killed, was concluded on Monday. From the evidence given it appeared that Ridgway, the en- i gine driver, had not until this summer driven over the Stockport and Blackpool route for more than a dozen years. A few days before the accident he made one trip successfully, but even then the fireman thought it necessary on approaching the Poulton curve to remind him that he must go slowly. Before proceeding on his second and fatal journey over the line Ridgway, it was stated, was " very cross." He did not like the idea of beisig sent to Blackpool again, and he told his wife that he should ask the foreman for a pilot to accompany him. The forettan said that no request of the kind was made. Evidence was called on behalf of the railway companies with the object of showing that a driver's familiarity with a certain route need not be seriously impaired by an absence of ten or a dozen years. The jury found ithat " the deceased met with death owing to culpable negligence on the part of the Lancashire and Yorkshire and the London and North-Western Joint Railway Companies in all4wing such a dangerous curve to continue on the main line, and in appointing a driver not sufficiently acquainted with the road." They further exonerated Ridgway from all blame.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.

• --- Sir,—The attention of the Committee of the Warring- ton Liberal Club has been called to certain letters which apooarod in the Warrington " Guardian "on tb• Bth ae 1 19th July. On behalf of the Committee I have to give an emphatic denial to the charges contained in the said letters and challenge he writer or writers to either prove the truthfulness of their statements at the earliest possible moment, or to publicly withdraw the charges and apologise for having made them.—On behalf of the Committee,
J. H. FLEMING, President.
THE CRISIS IN THE COAL TRADE.

Sir,—lt would be well for all parties, and the public in general, if this difficulty could be settled in an amic- able and satisfactory manner, without resorting to the suicidal policy of a strike. I know something of the effects of the late strike in the cotton trade and its terrible results, which to a great many people meant the loss of insurance policies, of household furniture, in many cases loss of health through insufficiency of food and warmth, and in some cases death as the result of privation and want. Let us hope that wise counsels may prevail and avert a similar calamity in the coal trade. As far as my observations go, the sympathy of the public is with the miners. The taking of one-fourth of the workman's wages—especially when that wage is a low one, as I understand by the papers it is not more than 18s. to 208. a week—is something terrible to con- template; and when we take into consideration the dangerous and exhaustive nature of the work, it seems as if everything was against the miner living a healthy life and seeing a "hale old age." He leaves home in the morning for his work, and what are the chances that lie rnay ever see that home alive again? How many miners have gone down the pit in the vigour of life in tke morning, but no night has ever seen their return— their working place has been their tomb. What, may I ask, has brought about the present crisis? If everybody paid as much for coal as I do, for the little I use the collier should get a good wage, aid the colliery proprietor a good profit. I live at Openshaw and pay for ordinary house coal 90. per cwt., or 153. 10d. a ton. There should be a good margin there for profit, which I suppose the middleman gets. Or does it come in this way. The supply far exceeds the demand. When it is known that certain property con- tains coal, speculators buy it, sink pits and get coal 3ut. That coal must be sold, and coal consumers are waited upon by one agent after another, endeavouring to do business, and underselling goes on, prices are cut down, until there is no margin for profit, except by reducing the wages of the miner, which are already too low. Cannot the colliery proprietors induce the public to pay more for their coal? They form combinations to reduce wages. Why cannot they combine to raise the price of coal and leave the wages alone ? lam perfectly wil- ling to stretch out another Ad. a cwt.-10d. a ton will be a good lift—and I ani not alone. It is. as far as I know, a general sentiment. How large consumers feel, I cannot say ; one thing I believe, and that is, tilos- a ould pay more rather than see a strike which would be :/ttle leas than ruin all round.

I hope this reduction may be averted. I have seen many reductions in my time in many trades, but ss. in the pound is, to me, an unheard of thing. Colliers are killed in many ways, but to starve them to death is both cruel and unjust in the extreme. I skould much like to see this dark cloud lifted ; there is anxiety enough in the collier's home every day without bringing in the gaunt wolf starvation to add to the many troubles of the miner and his family.—l am, sir, yours respectfullv,_
Sankey Bridges, July Eth, 1893.
CYMRO.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
A EHLETICS.
CRICKET.

Fora chanze I intended to have opened these notes with a little " first class cricket." But I cannot as it lias all been very third rate cricket this week. Indeed, perhaps I should be more correct if I said it was fourth class cricket—or not cricket at all. This at any rate may apply to the Warrington first eleven in their match with Birkenhead Park, on Saturday. They suffered a tlefeat which is conceded to be the mcst inglorio"as lick- ing they ever sustained. By dispassionate persons their play was described as being as bad as that of an aver- age school boy team. This is very hard, but I don't be., lieve it ; I don't seom to be able te craaa it into my head that any school boy team, no matter how hard they tried, no matter what experience they brought to bear, or with what native talent they backed it up, could have played a worse game.

The Warrington men took their innings first, and th• start seemed favourable enough for W. Podmore who lead off, scored 13 before he gave up his bat. No one knew then that the 13 was to be Warrinzton's " tallest" individual score ; nor did anyone know—not even the scorer—that the total score was to be 31. But it was so. It was not at all enlivebing to see the play that followed Podmore. Sugg and U. Clarke, and Bell all went out Isr 0. Then Clark offered a 1, Bibby followed with 2, J. J. Crostield with 4. Bolton with 1, and then it all closed up with duck eggs again, and the 31 was only made up by seven extras.

At the conclusion of the Warrington innings the spec- tators were not at all intent upon harbouring any secret indignation against their home players. They simply displayed it in exclamations of contumely and scathing derision. You could nearly see Warrington players blush for shame. But how was it when Birkenhead Park were half through their innings? I said Warrington people left after the Warrington innings, but now—well, there weren't any spectators left at all. Clarke commenced bowling in a prainising way, for he took two wickets successively for no runs. But he seemed to lose his style all at once and for the four wickets he took 88 runs were made. The same number of runs were made for five wickets taken by Crosfield. Then 18 piers were divided between five other bowlers who allowed 82 runs to be made and never took a wicket. But I didn't altogether agree with the division of, these overs. It seemed to me that Podmere ought to have been given a better chance, for it only required a little time to see the effects of his peculiar bowling.

It is true that the Warrington team was not a " choice" one ; but the question is why wasn't it? If there are good players in the club it is rather a hard thing—but a soft one for the opponents—that such a team as Birkenhead Park should be met with practically a second eleven team. Let Warrington remember the 202 against their 31, when they arrange their future teams.

The second eleven were practically beaten, too. They made 123 all out against 175 for hve wickets. The Bir- kenhead players were ail good hatsmen,one of them mak- ing 65, another 37, and another 34. They were either batsinen—or the Warzington bowlers were " off colour.'

Then descending among the juniors we find the order of the day is disorder in the way of scores. Sankey Wire Mills and Moore met. Sankey made 62 and Moore —oh, ye young Apollos f—they made 9. After this they will not feel very big, for they could not have been beaten much more (Moore) ! The Sankey players came out very well, especially Marshall and Hobson. There is a making of a good player in Marshall, many people think.

We arrive next at the match between Orford Crescent and Stockton Heath. The former scored 44, whilst Stockton Heath, despite the fact that they had the ser- vices of the Rev. Mr. Vernon, only managed to scrape together nine.

The Sankey Weslevans had an easy task in defeating Daniel's Balla, of St. Helens, for the second time this season. Not one of the Daniels reached double figures, the highest scorer being Eaves with nine. Watkins and Simpson did extremely well with the ball, each captur- ing tor wickets. For Sankey Bridges W. Bennett alone almost leached his opponents score, being ato his credit, E. Clare closely following with 22. From these agoras. however, there is a big drop. T. Brough with .seven not out coming third. There was quite a party who came with the St. Fieleners, and after the match, the members and friends of the two teams had a jolly time of it at the Sankey Bridges schoolroom where they sat down to tea,and.atterwards showed that their vocal attainments were not to be despised.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Look here, why don't the Warrington cyclists do something fresh? why don't they get out of this recent limpid, lazy, lagging, listless, lame fashion of theirs. The first thing that I got. to hear about the W. C. C. this week was, that they had been to Cranage again ! I shall be glad to hear when they finish studying local charts to find another place to go to. They seem to have got into a habit of getting on to their machines and machanically riding to Cranage. There is evidently a magnetic attraction.

Then we have the Warring,ton Wheelers. Well, good- ness only knows what has become of them. I was speaking to one member of the club, and he actually wasn't aware, for a time that there was such a club: - He said he'd forgotten all about it. The captain has hid to give up riding through overstraining himself in pacing, and altogether its very probable that by next season there will be no Wheelers Club in Warrington.

Here is a hint for the lady cyclists. Ladies flew right in the face of Mrs. Grundy by riding machines at all. But since then they have fl )wn up above her compre- hension by turning out with suitable riding costume. The latest fashion comes from Franca. It consists of short skirts, knoe breeches, and gaiters, very much like the costume worn in gymnasiums. Now this presents ' another opportunity for a Warrington lady cyclist to dis- tinguish herself. None of the lady riders have had enough courage to take the initiative in starting a club, but surely in the way of dress they are not lacking in initia- tory boldness?

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

I was glad to see that several Warrington athletes were again successful on Saturday,capturipg first prizes at important meetings. H.Webster, at the Salford Har- riers' Sports, took the 440 yards' hurdle from scratch comfortably. His form at the hurdle shows up better each week, and a good deal is expected of him in the future. At the Blackburn Rovers' F.C. Sports the 120 yards' race produced an exciting finish. A. J.Mottratn, known so favourably at the Gymnasium, landed home first by a few inches in front of Lumley, of Newcastle.

div.head: Bow Ls.
div.p: Bow Ls.

A very pleasant game of 15 up was played on the Liberal Club bowling green, on Saturday, between the Club team and Leigh Liberal Club team. The result was something to cheer the hearts of the home men—it was a victory by 59 points. I noticed that " Another" did a little better this week—indeed the whole team showed signs of imorovernent. Let them practice a little longer, an 1 they will soon understand the game, and— What ! They are veteran bowlers ? Well er-er —oh, I knew it all along.

In the Warrington and District League the Bull's Heat] team still keeps well anead. They have ten points, five more than any other team. Singular to say, however, all the matches an fa • have been very close ones, and ex- cellent play has be displayed. The following are the results up to Saturcidy : Played. Won. Loat. Drawn. Pt,. BuTs Head Cemetery Red Lion Horse aid Jockey. 5 Dank Quay

It was a " '' total with which the Newton-le-Wil- lows club beat Everton on Saturday. They won by 130 points, after which, the official report tells us with great simplicity, " they did adjourn for tea."
SWIMMING.

I learn that the Town Hall, Park and Baths Commit- tee have consented to allow the Swimming Club the free use of the baths on 30th August when the Northern Coun- ties Swimming Association semi-final polo match will be played. On that occasion there will also be an aqua- tic fete when races of a varied character will take place. The final polo match will take place at the same baths on the sth October' when another aquatic fete will be held. This ought to do the club some good, anyhow. Its membership at present, I learn, is 70.

Some time next week the ladies' baths will be opened. I think! can see some of the " sex " smile their sweetest now. The fee in the first class bath will be 6d. and the season ticket 15s. ; in the second class bath the entrance fee will be 3d. and season tickets will cost ss. each. All kinds of facilities will be given to female school teachers to learn to swim and to bring female scholars.

div.head: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT THE WIDNES RANGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT THE WIDNES RANGE.
RE.SULTS OF THE COMPETITIONS.

The Ist V.B.South Lancashire (Warrington) Re- giment, commenced their annual shooting competi- tions on Saturday and Monday last, at the Widnes range. The officers present on Saturday were Cap- tains Ridgway, Buckton, Chorley,and Appleton,aud Sergeants-instructor Woodin and Barker. There were about 80 persons present. Three competitions should have been held on Saturday, but there was only time for one, and the remaining two were held on Monday. FIRST COMPETITION.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

The monthly meeting of the committee of the Runcorn Free Library was . held on Wednesday morning at the Town Hail, under the presidency of Mr. Riley. The Librarian submitted his report for the month, showing that there had been issued 948 volumes in the lending department, an increase of 116 on the corresponding period last year; and 23 in the reference library, increase 14. The Librarian, in his eleventh annual report, stated that the reading room, which was. supplied with an in- teresting collection of papers, periodicals, and maga- zines, had proved a great advantage to increasing num- bers of readers of both sexes. The additions to the library during the past year amounted to 702 volumes, 517 of which were purchased and 185 presented. The total number of volumes was 8.938. Among the books presented were 182 volumes of technical works, the generous gift of Mr. J. T. Brunner,M.P. These supplied a long-felt need, as the library was specially weak in works of that class. It was hoped that the students of technology in the town would make the utmost use of the works now placed within their reach. The bor- rowers' tickets now issued during the year numbered 704, a decrease or 31 as compared with last year. The alterations with regard to the hours when the library was open had been greatly appreciated, and the crowd- ing at the windows had been reduced to a minimum. The library had been open for the issue of books 193 days, and 21,649 works had been takm out during the year, being 108 fewer than last year. The average daily issue was 112. References were made to the course of lectures delivered during the winter, and then it was stated that the necessity for their continuance during the coining season had been obviated by the adoption of a course which the committee had succeeded in obtain- ing from the Gilchrist Educational Trust, and which would be delivered fortnightly in the Public Hall. The committee expressed their thanks to the donors of money, books, periodicals, and newspapers, without whose help it would be difficult to carry oa the institu- tion with efficiency. The report was approved.

et ion probably, made his first, atterzpt at lyirg— nud it was a clumsy one. He said we hrol teen fishing near Wigan and had had such luck that all our bait and hooks were gone. Then they said let us show them our lish—wriat we had caught. And Thompson blandly told them—l liked him for the attempt !—that we had sent them by train to the market. Poor fellow, he couldn't understand why his lie wasn't accepted, like those told every day by his friends. But we had our revenge ultimately. After half an hour's futile attempts to catch fish, Thompson hit on a happy plan. We were forty yards from our friends. Thompson picked up an old salmon can and slit two pieces of tin from it of a semi-circular shape and then fastened them to our lines. We dipped them in stealthily, alid then snatched the line with a yell ! The tin had a pale silvery look which made our friends think we were drawing deice. We did this a dozen times in 20 minutes, our friends regarding us with considerable envy. Presently one of them said: "What bait are you using?" " Worms."

He promptly changed his bait. We went on pull- ing the tin out, and pretending to till the basket. But the man with the worm bait did not have a bite. By-and-by the other man said:— "Did you say you were using worms?" "Oh, no! paste." The first one opened his mouth to say something, but followed his friend's example and baited with paste. In a while we decided to go, back home, and Thompson strapped on the basket and as we paused to bid our friends goodbye they complained of their ill-luck. Thompson asked them what they had got on their lines and they said with surprise " Why paste, of course I" " Yell" he replied, whilst they looked up expectantly "You don't want that on your line to fill the basket." "What do we want." " Why, yo—yo—you want some fish on." Ali ! well, we left them, and bought some fish from a keeper to take home. We said we caugbt these—l didn't tell them what else I'd caught at the time, hut they found out by and by; it was rheumatism. , Thompson had brain fever for a time, and whilst ' his brain was thus disordered he sued for a divorce from his wife. With these experiences in mind I dscline to take any more angling.

div.head: FISHING EXPEDITION.
div.p: A FISHING EXPEDITION.
"ANOTHER SIDE OF THE QUESTION."
Br LUKE BLUNT.

Only the other week a friend of mine tried to I persuade me to join in a fishing expedition. But I declined vehemently, emphatically. Sp exasperated am I at times about the false, systematically col,- structed fallacies relating to the alleged enjoy- , ' ments of angling, that when I hear of a length hav- ing too much water for its fish, as happened last week, I want to demonstrate my joy. I want to prance around and shout " Hooray.' The Warring- ton anglers must not take this as a display of pre- judice against them, for it isn't. I speak from the heart; I speak as one who has been sold ; as one who has been ensnared into the toils of a gigantic fraud. I have seen " the other side of the ques- tion." I have seen that what some people consider pleasure—the waste of patience, the contraction of chills, and other things—are privations to others. To prove this I will relate the facts of a fishing expedition in which I joined one day last year. These facts may seem extraordinary, but there are several well-known fishermen in Warrington, who can corroborate them. Whether they are true or not, they will corroborate them, anyway, because I know. I related the incidents a week after- wards when I was lying on a sick bed; I think it was a sick bed—but, at anyrate, I was lying.

Newton Lake was the place selected for the ex- pedition. Thompson and myself decided to go by the 11-op.m. train to Newton, and fish during the night—for it was summer, and the nights for weeks past had been balmy and warm. Ile had prepared all the bait, and that morning had packed up a large fishing basket with food and hooks, and all necessary implements and articles for both ourselves and the fish to participate in. The arrangement was that we should meet at the station; but as the evening grew into night I began to feel uneasy about Thompson. 1 felt sure he would oversleep himself, or go and do something to cause us to miss the. train. Se at nine o'clock 1 determined to set out for Stockton Heath, where he lived, and thus see that he got through all right. I hurried him up and we set out for the station at ton o'clock. He strapped the large basket on my back, and carried the rods himself, and ;as we trudged along the weight of my burden became so unbearable that if it had not been for the fear of seeming to be effeminate and weak I should have asked him to take a turn. But I stood it to the best of my ability—and perspired and groaned and ; puffed and panted till we reached the station. We ; climbed Onto the platform,and lo! there was a train just about to leave. We did not look at the time-- this would not have been in keeping with anything that happened on that infernal expedition—because , we should have seen that it was only a quarter to eleven. No, we leaped into the train as the engine whistled ; a porter shouted " where are you for." We replied " Newton," and were just able to catch , his answer as see glided out of the station. He said : This train doesn't stop before Wigan ! My friend was not angry with me; he was grave and fatherly, and told me never to go about hurrying people, because that was just what would happen, every time. Ile confessed that he might have looked at the time, but added that had he not been hurried he should have walked into the right train without so much trouble as we had expended in getting into the wrong one. I commenced to argue, but he closed me up with : " Luke, don't be an ass. You know if you hadn't been so confoundedly sharp in i.umping in here, we should have got in the next train, so where's the use of arguing: i didn't seem to know, and closed up like a love-sick cockle. By and by he said we would unstrap the basketand make ourselves comfortable with a little supper, because we should have to walk from Wigan to Newton. He told me not to be down-hearted, and to always take little accidents philosophically. Then he opened the basket. The next moment he leaped from it with dilating eyes and gasped : " ! crickey ! Here's ii go." "What is it?' I said.
" What is it? Look at it—gaze at it." I looked in the basket and saw it was full of potatoes. But I turned to him placidly and asked:—
" Well, what are they good for ?" " IVhat are they good for—look at them." OI did, and said with innocent frankness:—
"Are they piscatorial inducements?" " Piscatorial inducements be IP •

Then he slammed the basket under the seat, and put his head out of the window. lie is a religious man. Ile is either a Sunday school superintendent —or his mother does the washing for the minister, at any rate, I know he is religious. I could not de- tect what words he uttered so fiercely to the dark night, but I'm sure his feet were swearing from the way they moved. When he had untosomed himself he came and sat down again, and lighted his pipe, and presently his rage thawed beneath the soothing appeals of Lady Nicotine,and the warmth of his heart beamed forth again in a smile on his face. He simply said : " Well, it is a joke." He remem- bered his wife had borrowed the bas Let to bring some potatoes in, and had forgctten to empty it ana•replace the other articles.. Then .1..t00, said it was a joke—for his wife. ,

We arrived at Wigan at midnight—the hour when the ppet tells us graveyards gape—with returning life, not with sleepiness. It was raining, too. We ' trudged through the town with our spirits damped —and our apparel well watered. The potatoes had been emptied on the road—it was a cruel waste ; but it would have been a more cruel waste—of la- bour—had we carried them. Just as we were leav- ing the town and about to dive into the dark wilderness of rain and lampless lanes and fields, Tnompson uttered a dramatic " Ah-a "; and took from his breast pocket a flask. And in the yellow, sickly light of the last glimmering gas lamp he drank " good health." Before he could withdraw the flask from his mouth three _tall colliers were standing before us grinning. -- " Wetting it insoide, la-ad," said one. To which Thompson said he was ; the collier said it was a nice flask, and Thompson said yes. The collier said " Lemme look at un." Thompson said it didn't amount to anything, it wasn't much —but his grandmother had left him no slouch of a flask that he bad at home; and he'd bring that and let them look at it, some day. The collier said they didn't." dig "for " groodmoothers," so he'd see that flask. And they emptied it, after which the tallest one said they would go and fill it; and then they went away from us. This was another of the boasted pleasures of fishing I Oh, how my heart swelled with bitter, bitter rage ! How can I describe the miserable tramp, through the sludgy dark country roads? It was like a night in purgatory—only wet- ter. For two long hours we dragged our weary limbs along, never seeming to get nearer our destination; for two long hours we swam in torrents of rain,and at length we reached a wayside viLa.and we sneaked throukh the • garden gate, and sank exhausted and disgusted on to the mat in the porch. We sheltered here. Thompson still tried to bear up against our tribulations; he even tried to cheerme but his sham philosophy wits flimsy; his show of good spirits was shallow; and his forced laugh was a hollow mockery, for I could see that what he wanted was to ease his feelings ,by being set at large with a pellet gun, and some colliers and un- thinking housewives, and precipitate connanions. We each tried to court slumber, cold and wet as we were, but Thompson tossed and complained, and then gave it up. Ile had an idea that I could not sleep. But when he saw me trying to dose off he pretended that he thought I was asleep. He patted me on the head in a needlessly vigorousmanner,and said : " Poor fellow !—sleep on good heart, you need it. He's not used to these hardships, so I'll not disturb him." Then he accidentally stumbled against me, and was happy when I opened my eyes. Once I forced an artifical snore. He tried the old game on, patting me and speaking like the comic man in the drama does to the homeless heroine. I didn't budge. He tired of this and sat and watched me for a quarter of an hour. Then he lost his tem- per and said " Here wake UM. This is neither the place nor time for sleeping." "Oh, get a nap," I said. " Here, if you're used to sleeping on door steps, do you think Pm a vagabond." " Well," I said, " I never said you were, but I shouldn't like to —to say—you—weren't:llo got mad at that,and the result was that an argument arose and grew in strength like a storm,till at length a creaking noise on the stairs, and a glimmering light in the keyhole warned us to go away. And we went.

Well. we reached Newton Lake about seven o'clock, I tie most miseratde pair of animated dish oltw.t,,t hat could have been imagined. And all we had t) fill with were our rods withont bait or hooks. We found sitting contentedly on the bank two friends who had arranged to come by the early train that morning. They said "where had we been," and Thompson thinking to avett any humili

div.head: SAD FATALITY TO A WARRINGTON
div.p: SAD FATALITY TO A WARRINGTON
SCHOOL BOY.
SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A DRIVER.
THE INQUEST ADJOURNED.

Thomas Smith, six years and nine m-nths old, on of a widow living at No. 73, Pierpoint-street, left Wycliffe Day School shortly after four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon for the purpose of returning home. While standing in the middle of the street opposite the school he became confused by the proximity of a couple of horses and spring carts. He was unable to get back to the footpath, and was knocked down by one of the horses. He got up, walked two or three yards, and then fell to the ground. Several p,rsons saw the accident, and one of them, P.S. Lawrence, ran up to the lad, picked him up, and carried him into Dr. • Adams' surgery, where the poor little fellow died in about five minutes. An inquest was held on the body, at the Police Court Parade Room, on Friday afternoon, conducted by Mr. Brighouse, coroner. It was alleged that the cart which knockrd the deceased down belonged to Mr. .1. Toole, marine store dealer, and Mr. A. Browne watched the inquiry on behalf of Mr. Toole. . _

Mrs: Sarah Smith, mother of the deceased, was the fast witness called. She said she last saw her son alive a few minutes before eight o'clock on Tuesday morning, when he left home for Wycliffe School. He did not com• home to his dinner as usual. The next thin,' she heard about him Wel3 that he was lying dead at Dr. Adams' surgery. Richard Griffiths, of Wallace's Court, Church-street, Faid that on the afternoon in question he was driving a coal cart along Bewsey-Areet towards Tanners-lane. There was another cart about 14 or 15 yards behind him, fie saw the deceased run into the read, appar- ently with the intention of crossing to the other side. He passed between witness's cart and the other one, which belonged to Mr. Plinstone. At that time another cart was coming along in the opposite direction, and was driven by a youth, who was the son of Mr. Toole,marine store dealer. The deceased boy corns into contact with this cart and was knocked down. The driver shouted to the boy but he was unable to pull up. He did not think that the driving of either Plinstone or the boy was " furious."

oole, aged 12, son of Mr. John Toole, said he was driving his father's spring cart along Bewsey-road, at the time named. He was accompanied by his two younger brcthers. As he passed the coal cart driven by Griffiths he saw the deceased run from behind his cart, but lie did not know that anything had happened him until he beard a shout, and upon turning round saw the deceased lying in the road.—The Coroner : What did you do then.-1 drove home. I was excited.—The Coroner : You were excited because you had run over the lad I suppose ?—No sir, I did not run over him. I don't think so.—The Coroner : Then what made you excited and drive home. • What did you do when you gut home ?—I told my mother that a boy was run over.— The Coroner : Did you tell her you had run over him ? No sir.—lnspector Bowen: Did you not think you had run over him ?—No.—lnspector Bowen : Then what made you excited ?—I don't know, I'm sure.—A Jury- man : Probably one of the other youths had told him what had happened.—The Coroner : Did you not see the deceased run into your cart.—No sir, I did not.— The Coroner : Did you feel the jolt, as if you had run over something.—No sir.—The witness was further ex- amined and told " not to be afraid of that gentleman— the coroner, and to tell the truth." He simply recapitu- lated his former statement. Finally the Coroner said : " Come here my boy," and having brought the witness to his table he tried to induce Min to tell the" whole truth." the boy seemed very much concerned and very nervous, but despite all sorts of re-assuring statements he was induced to say nothing except that he simply saw deceased run from behind Griffiths cart, and then hearing the cry turned round and saw him lying on the road.

Dr. Adams in giving evidence said that deceased was brought to his surgery by Sergeant Lawrence. He ad- ministered a draught to him but he died in a few moments afterwards. Upon an examination of the clothes and also the external part of the body he was convinced that the boy had not been run over. The Coroner: Oh ! Hew do you account for it.—Dr. Adam!, Upon a further examination—a post mortent—l tound that the deceased had died from dislocation of the neck caused by the upward removal of the skull. There were no external marks of injury about him, nothing to show that he was run over, except that his face was somewhat bruised ana his teeth dislodged, which showed that something had struck him violently in the face. . .

Mrs. Mary Burke, Gee-st., said that at the time the accident occurred she was in Bewsey-st.,looking for one of her children who was lost. She saw two carts com- ing down towards her one was Plinston's and the other was Griffiths. She also saw another cart driven by a boy going in the opposite direction. She saw the de- ceased boy run across into the middle of the street, and get between the cart driven by the boy and the one driven by a man—Plinston's. Plinston was driving very quickly and was swearing. 'lhe boy got between Puns- ton's trap and Toole's and seemed to be confused. The man who was driving Plinstnn's cart stood up and shouted but before the boy could get out of the way the horse with I'linston's cart had dashed against him and knocked him dovrn.—The Coroner : You are sure it was not the cart driven by the boy ?—Yes sir, quite sure. The Coroner : This seems very lemarkable. Call Griffiths again. Griffiths upon being called said he was sure that it was Toole,: cart which knocked deceased down. Plinston's cart was 100 yards away. . _ .

Mrs. Burke : No it Was not. It was only about 14 yards frma the coal cart. The man who was driving was swearing and driving at a high speed. Sergeant Lawrence, employed by Pearson and Knowles, stated that he picked the youth up after the accident occurred. His attention was directed to the boy by hearing a shout,and when he turned round he saw the deceased rise from the toad, stagger two steps and then fall on to his face. He ran and picked him up; his face was pall, his fists were el•enclied,and hjs eyes were wide open and fixed as though he was dead. He ran with him ta Dr. Adams' surgery, and Dr. Adams said, " Lawrence this is it sad case."i He did not see the ac- cident occur, but he thought that the deceased was not knocked down by Plinston's cart. Inspector Bowen at this juncture stated that a little girl who was outside had seen the accident occur. The child was brought in. She said her name was Annie Turton, 12 years if age, and a scholar at Wycliffe Schools. She gave her evidence in a very terse and clear style. The deceased boy she said,was running across the street when he got "fixed" between the two carts—Plinston's and 'l'oole's. He seemed to be confused as to how to get away, and before he could move Mr. Plinston's horse, which was running very quickly dashed up against him, and knocked him down. In answer to cross-examinations she said she knew Mr. Plinston perfectly well, and lie was driving. She was quite sure it was his horse and not Toole's which knocked the boy down. The Coroner : This is very serious. The inquiry must be adjaurned and Plinston brought before us, as well as the two boys who were with Toole. These trap acci- dents are becoming too common, and I must point out again, as I have done before that drivers have only a secondary claim to the road. They are in charge of dangerous things, and upon them rests the responsibility of seeing that accidents do not happen. lam very sorry to say, however, that they do not recognise this. and it is now the pedestrian who has to look out and not the driver. In the west of Lancashire, this negli- gence is most glaring. , The inquest was adjourned until Mord
afterno•ri.
MAYORAL GARDEN: PARTY" AT CAMP

Mr. Alderman F. U. Oossage, J.P., . Mayor of Widnes, gave a garden party at his residence Camp Woolton, on Thursday afternoon. His Worship had invited about 700 to partake of his hospitality, and the majority accepted the invitation. The list I incladed tne aldermen, the councillors, and corpo- rate officials, the clergy and medical profession, 1 many of the tradesmen of the town, and a number of gentlemen who, although not residing within the borders of Hal new borough, have had large, and still COntiDUP to have considerable interests in the town and ' trade. With commendable enterprise,the Cheshire Lines Railway Company ran a special train at 4.5 p.m. for Hough Green,by which nearly 300 ladies and gentlemen travelled, but the full fare was exacted. Many of the guests travelled by private and public conveyance, and about live hundred ladies and gentlemen would be pre- sent. On alighting at Hunt's Cross, an , enterprising Widnes livery stableman had a number of cabs and i other vehicles n readiness to carry the visitors to Camp Hill, and as there were no lack of fares,no doubt he was well repaid for his trouble. A considerable number, however, walked to their destination. The Mayor and Mayoress received their numerous guests in the drawing room, extending to each a hearty hand shak• and a cordial gee, ting. This pleasant function fulfilled, the guests proceeded through the open window to the lawn, whence a tine lands.mpe opened before them. In the foreground is a short stretch of well-wooded country, with the Mersey at the border, like a siver streak, and the fruitful plains of Cheshire beyond, the everlasting hills of the Principality of Wales forming a magnificent background. This prospect enjoyed to the full, a stroll was taken through the extensive kitchen garden, thence to the glass houses where plants and blaoms were seen to perfection ; and grapes and peaches were depending from the branches in rich abundance. Tropical plants, orchids and ferns there were in profusion, to delight the sense of sight, and a grotto of exquisite beauty formed fitting, conclusion to the saunter through the hothouses in which these rare plants were to be seen. En route might be noticed a building, apparently used as the gardener's office, the walls and part of the ceiling a which was covered with cards recording the prizes which have been won by the plants and blooms from Mr. Gossage's gardens. After this stroll, a walk to the refreshment tent in the park opposite the house formed a pleasant change, and the good things were admirably dispensed by the steward of the Liverpool Reform Club and his assistants. There was also a large marquee in which thoie who were in need of a rest might retire, and Sit in the shade beyond the beat of the glorious sun which brightened the whole surroundings into a beauti- ful picture. The delights of music were not wanting. On the lawn Eyton's string band from Liverpool i performed a selection of music n admirable style. The prize brass band of Messrs. Gossage and 'Sons, under the conductorship of Mr. J. Broady, also delighted numer- ous auditors with an excellent programme. As seven o'clock approached the guests began to return towards the Elizabethian Mansion, which is the house of one of the merchant princes of Widnes, and " Good-be" hav- ing been pronounced to the Chief Magistrate and his lady, the homeward way was travelled as quickly as Possible ; and the drear wastes of Widnes exchanged for the sylvan glades of Camp Hill. The whole function was of the most enjoyable character, and the memory ef it will linger for many days to come in the minds of all those who were privileged to be there.

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the members of this so- ciety was held in the Bethesda Lecture hall, on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance of ladies and gentlemen. 3lr. J. Brundrit, J.P., the president, occupied the chair. Mr. W. H. Rogerson read the annual report prepared by Mr. James Booth, the hon. sec. The report stated that the first season had been a successful one. It would be remembered that in 'September last the society was placed in a very awkward position, owing to the want of a conductor. The solution of the difficulty was lelt in the hands of the newly-appointed committee,who at once set to work to fill up the vacancy; and not being able to meet with a suitable amateur, get into com- munication with various professionals, and finally Mr. Frank R. Crossley, of Warrington; was selected for recommendation to the society, and at a subsequent meeting was unanimously appointed. He (the sec.) was sure that every member of the society would readily admit that they had no reason to regret making that appointment—(applause)—and would be pleased with the efficient and courteous manner in which Mr. Crossley had conducted the society during the past season. After describing the several concerts,the report prooeeded to state that the society had reason to be proud of the support that had been accorded by the vice-presidents, and also by the public generally. At the present time there were 99 vice-presidents' names on the books, which spoke well for the interest. shown. With regard to the singing members, he was sorry to report a falling off in numbers. At the close of the season 1891-2 the chorus numbered 96 ; this season 85,a decrease of 11. This was a small number for a society whioh had so many advantages. It was to be hoped that there might be a considerable advent of new mem- bers next season. To those musically inclined—and there were many such in Runcora—a most enjoyable way of improving and using the talent they might pos- sess, was offered by the weekly rehearsals of this so- ciety. . . .

Alr. Frank Scott, the hon. treasurer, produced the balance sheet, and stated that the year commenced with a balance in band of £3 103. 6d., the amount subscribed by the president, vice-presidents, and members was £ll9 33. 61. ; the tickets s.ild for the three concerts realised £64 63. 10d. ; chairs sold to the l'ublic Hall Company, £6 103. ; half profit on programmes ,501d,155.; music sold by Librarian, £ll 51. 4d. ; making in all a total of £205 us. 21. The payments included an item of £97 133. for fees for artists, and conductor paid for hire of Public Hall and other rooms, £2l 19s. ; orehestra including hire of pianos, £4O Os. 6d. ; miscellaneous items, £44 133. 6d. There was a balance to the credit of the Society of Ll 16s. Bd. The President proposed the adoption of both reports, and in doing so congratulated the Society upon coming out in such glowing colours. They started with a larger balance than they had at the finish, but, this was their first venture with a professional conductor : they had had to pay for his services and it showed that there was much vitality in the Society. Under these circumstances it was hardly necessary to debate at that meeting whether the Society should continue for another year, And they had better now look upon it as a permanent institution and carry it on as such. (Applause.) Ile hoped that the interest and support of the vice-presidents would be maintained, because without them the Society could not ,to on, and lie thought that would not only be a pity hut a calamity. He referred to the pleasures afforded by the Society not only to the members hut to those who were listeners, and expressed the hope that the Society would be more successful in the future than the past.—Mr. Joseph Littler seconded the motion, expressing his concurrence with the Chairman's re- marks.— I he reports were unanimously adopted. Mr. John Birkett moved a vote of thanks to the Com- mittee and the honorary officers for their services dur- ing the past year. They deserved their hearty thanks. (Applause.)—Mr. W. Jones seconded the proposition which was carried.—Mr. Littler responded. Mr. Littler moved the re-appointment of Mr. Brun- drit as president. They could not get a better gentle- man for the position, He had been connected with the musical life of the town for a large number of years and it was impossible to say how much he had done for this society. (Applause.) Mr. W. 11. Frith seconded, re- marking that Mr. Brundrit had taken very great interest in the welfare of the society. The resolution was carried unanimously.. Mr. Brundrit on resuming the chair was loudly applauded, and in acknowledging the renewed honour they had conferred upon him, said he should do his best to promote the interest of the society. (Applause.) Be trusted the vice president and those subscribers who were so, helpful last year. would come forward in the same good spirit this year. (Ap- plause.) On the proposition of the President, seconded by Mr. W. Crosby, the vice-presidents were re-elected es bloc.

The president proposed the re-appointment of Mr. Crossley.as conductor, and referred to his services in very eulogistic terms. He had acted in a courteous,and gentlemanly manner to the whole of the members, and he had rendered the chorus very efficient.—Mr. W. B. Pierpoint seconded the motion, and said not only had Mr. Crossley displayed great musical ability, and done the best possible for the society, but the receipts of the society had increased. That was a very gratifying re. stilt from a business point of view.—Mr. Littler sup- ported the motion which was carried by acclamation which was repeated when Mr. Crossley entered the room. Mr.Crossley heartily thanked the members for his re-election. The work besides being a matter of business and profit, was also a labour of love, and lie should be very sorry indeed to have to give it up. He gratefully acknowledged the help he had received in his work dur- ing the past season from the officials and others, and he specially mentioned Mrs. W. B. Kay, the accompanist. to whom he moved a special vote of thanks.—Mr. Scott seconded.—Carried. Mr. Kay replied on behalf of his wife. _ _

The following appointments wore made : hon. secre- . taries, Messrs. J. Booth and W. H. Rogerson, hon. 'treasurer, Mr. F. Scott ; orchestral secretary, Mr. W. B. Kay ; librarian, Mr. J. Marlow; accompanist, Mrs. W. R. Kay ; organist, Mr. J. Musgrove ; Committee, Misses Comerford, Crosby, Wrigfit and Stubbs ; Messrs. J. Littler, W. Handley, R. W. Pierpoint, W. B. Frith and C. Pownall ; auditors Mr. T. Handley and Mr. J. Hirkett.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.
