div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
HATTENING ON A CHESHIRE FARMER

--- Some malicious person took ten or a doz2n iron pins and drove them into the ground in a grass field ready for mowing, belonging to Mr. Edwards, of Permlon, Cheshire. When the tnan came to cut the bay he was repeatedly stopped dead, and the knives of the machine injured by the rods. The outrage is attributed to some person who objects to the machine as labour-saying appliances.

div.head: FRANCE AND KAM.
div.p: FRANCE AND KAM.

In the Rouse of Commons yesterday, in reply to Sir Ellis Ashmead Bartlett, Sir Edward Grey said he did not think it would conduce to a friendly settlement of the matter if her Majesty's Government were to endeav- our to induce the French Government to extend the period given to the Siamese Government in which to reply to the ultimatum. In answer to Mr. Curzon, the Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs said the Government expected to hear from Lord Dufferin shortly what were the geographic& , limitations laid down by the French in regard to the cession to France of territory on the left bank of the Mekong river. Wnether the cession would injuriously effect British interests and trade in Blitish Bnrmai. ' could not yet be said.

div.head: HORRIBLE STORY-IF TRUE,
div.p: HORRIBLE STORY-IF TRUE,
CONVERTING A BABY INTO PIE MEAT.

-- - PARIS FRIDAY.—A horrible story is reported from Lille, where a butcher, named Louis Grimonprez and h 6 mistress, Fiore Lezy, have been arrested on a charge or killing their child and using its body in their businesh of making meat pies. The details have only just been disclosed by an assistant of Grimonprez, with whom be hes had a quarrel, though the crime was committed in February last. The employe Taughe says that Fiore Lezy was secretly confined, and that Grimonprez killed the infant by breaking its back across his knee. He then offered 'Fantle 50 frincs, to make away with Ulf body, but lie refused. Then Taughe says his master threw the body into the large pan which was used for boiling meat, and that it was subsequently ueed with the rest in making a pate. Grimonprez threatened to kill Taughe if he breathed a word of what he had seen.

div.head: CRISIS IN THE COAL TRADE.
div.p: THE CRISIS IN THE COAL TRADE.

conference between the representatives of the Miners' National Federation and the colliery owners took place yesterday in the Westminster Palace Hotel. The proceedings wore strictly private, but it is understood that the miners' delegates reported the resolutions of the recent miners' conference at pirminghain to resist the proposed reduction of wages, and a strike is regarded as inevitable.

div.head: MINERS' VERSION OF TFIE CASE.
div.p: MINERS' VERSION OF TFIE CASE.

Mr. T. Glover, J.P., miners' agent, St. Helens, writes combatting the statement that the proposed reduction of 25 per cent, means only 2s. a week in the miners wages, as the 25 per cent, would only be taken off previous in- creases. Such a statement, he says, is very misleading. " The miners," he points out, " are paid so much per 'ton, and in some places instead they are paid so much per yard. Now if a miner has 10 ton at is. per ton, and 5 yards at 2s. per yard, that will make £1 altogether, I then the percentage is put upon thr £l,and if the miners suffer 25 per cent, it will come off the £l. so that you will see that it will mean ss. out Of the £l. Again, it is asserted that there are more men getting under than £1 per week. The same thing applies to the miners ot St. Helens. There is a large number in St. Helens gett- ing under £1 per week. The miner: of St. Helens,along with all theiither miners connected with the Federation of Great Britain believe that the miners' wages are low enough, and we do not think the employers are justified in asking us for a 25 per cent, reduction in wages be- cause they have reduced the price of coal'. Who have they reduced the coal to ? Not to the householders, as they have to pay 10s., 123., and as high as 153. per ton; but they have allowed a reduction to the railway com- panies, who have raised the tariff 20 to 30 per cent. And yet they allow them to have their coals is. to 13.6 d. per ton cheaper. The same thing applies to the gas com- panies and shipping companies, whc are able to pay 6 to 30 per cent, dividend in some cases. Does not such action on the part of the employers in allowing those who are able to pay a fair price for coal to have it cheaper show that the employers are to blame? and after they have done so they come to the ,workmen and ask them to suffer a reduction of 25 per cent. '

PREPARING FOR THE STRIKE. A West Hartlepool correspondent telegraphs :—Con- sequent upon the threatened great strike of colliers, in which the Northumberland and Durham men will not participate, the mine owners here are entering into con- tracts for tho conveyance of coal by sea to districts affected by the stoppage. One large shipowner of West Hartlepool lia.s been asked to provide steamers for the shipment of from 10,000 to 15,000 tons to the port of Hull alone, and similar orders are expected in other quarters.

div.head: NAVAL MANCEITVRES.
div.p: THE NAVAL MANCEITVRES.
ANOTHER DISASTER NARROWLY AVERTED.

A magnificent sight was witnessed at Falmouth, on Thursday morning, when the three squadrons, which comprise sixty-one vessels, left in fine weather. There were twenty-seven large warships,comprising the A and B Red Squadrons, and ten cruisers, torpedo catchers, and twenty-four torpedo boats, forming the Irish Coat squadron. While the B fleet were approaching Fahnouth from Milford Haven, and steaming in two lines. on IVednesday evening, the signal was made, " alter course sixteen points." Apparently the signalman hoisted the wrong pennant, as,had the manceuvre been cart ied out, a collision would have been almost inevitable, with pro- bably a repetition of the Victoria disaster. Rich ship, however, kept its answering pennant at the dip,meaning i that, the signal was not understood, and this caused the admiral to negative the original order, and to give ttis signal, " Turn outwards," instead of "inwards,"

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISC:ASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878. AND 1886. SWINE FEVER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Friday, the 14th day of July, 1893.— IT WAS ORDERED that, from and after the 24th day of July instant, the Regulations made by the said Exe- cutive Committee on the 18th day of January, 1893, shall be extended, and apply to the COUNTY OF SOMERSET, and such Regulations shall be read and construed as if the said County of Somerset had been originally included therein. The effect of this Order is that Swine ARE ABSOLU- TELY PROHIBITED from being moved into the District of this Local Authority FROM THE COUNTY OF SOMERSET, except for the special purpose mentioned in the said Regulations made on the 18th January,lB93, and then only in accordance with the Conditions named in such Regulations. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 17th July, 1893.

LUBBOCK, Mr. GLADSTQNE said it was not at present proposed to issue gold against rupees.—Mr. EvEriETT asked whether in view of the larger demand which the proposed new monetary policy in India would create for gold, and of the consequent possible further rise in the value of that metal, and proportionate further fall in the prices of commodities measured by it,both here and in the Colonies he would give Parliament the opportunity of discussing the matter before finally establishing a hold standard in in India.—Mr. GLADSTONE said he was not able to ac- cede to the assumptions which were contained in the question, but apart from those assumptions he thought he might point out that the Indian financial statement would afford opportunity for discussing the policy re- cently adjourned. RUSSIANS ON THE INDSAN FRONTIER.—The Under. Secretary for foreign affairs stated that there was, as far as the Government was aware, no foundation for the statement that, an armed Russian force had been ordered into the Pamir on the strategic line, leading towards the North Indian frontier. THE POET LAUREATE APPOINTMENT—The Prime Min- ister stated that at present there was no intention to fill up the vacant post of Poet Laureate. HOME RULE FINANCE.—The House resumed Committee on the new clause of the Government of Ireland Bill.
